4.5 The Cotton Corporation of India Ltd. (CCI) has been nominated by the 
Government of India for undertaking MSP operations, in the event kapas prices of 
seed cotton (kapas) fall below the MSP level, for procuring kapas offered by the 
cotton farmers in various APMC market yards at MSP rates without any quantitative 
limit. Before the commencement of the Cotton Year (Oct. to Sept.), every year, the 
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) recommend the MSP based on 
the formula of 1.5 times the cost of production (A2+FL) to ensure reasonably fair 
remuneration, i.e., at least 50% over the cost of production, to farmers. Accordingly, 
taking into consideration the recommendation of CACP, the Ministry of Agriculture 
declares MSP for two basic varieties of Fair cotton, viz. medium staple length (staple 
length of 24.5 mm to 25.5 mm and micronaire value of 4.3 to 5.1) and long staple 
length (staple length of 29.5 to 30.5 mm and micronaire of 3.5 to 4.3). For Cotton 
Season 2025-26, MoA & FW has fixed MSPs for fair-grade cotton at ₹ 7710/- per 
quintal for medium staple and ₹ 8110/- per quintal for long staple cotton.  
4.6 Based on the Support Price of these two basic varieties of Seed cotton (Kapas) 
and considering the quality differential, normal price differential and other relevant 
factors, the MSP for other classes of Fair Seed cotton (Kapas) is fixed by the Textile 
Commissioner of India. 
4.7 In India, out of an estimated 6 million cotton farmers, about 85% are marginal 
and small farmers with less than 2 hectares. Factors such as crop damage due to 
adverse agro-climatic conditions (e.g., insufficient or untimely rains, floods, 
hailstorms) and natural calamities reduce yields and increase production costs for 
cotton farmers. 
To overcome the above situation and to provide an alternate channel to sell cotton at 
a predetermined reasonable price, the Government of India declares MSP of cotton 
every year based on the formula of 1.5 times the cost of production (A2+FL), to 
ensure reasonably fair remuneration, i.e. at least 50% over the cost of production to 

23 
 
farmers. The main objective of MSP is to prevent distress sales by cotton farmers by 
providing an alternative price at which cotton can be sold. The MSP system ensures 
a minimum price for cotton farmers and protects them from distress sales when 
cotton prices fall below the MSP. 
4.8 According to the Ministry of Textiles, major MSP operations for cotton were 
conducted in 2014-15, 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2024-25 by CCI, with volumes 
ranging from 92 lakh bales to 125 lakh bales and values ranging from around  
₹ 19,500 crore to ₹ 37,437 crore. The volume of MSP operations for cotton largely 
depends on the demand and supply conditions in domestic and international 
markets. The quantum of procurement and the number of beneficiaries tend to 
change each year, depending on market conditions.

V. HANDLOOM SECTOR 
 
5.1 The Handloom Sector is one of the largest unorganized economic activities of 
India and it constitutes an integral part of the rural and semi- rural livelihood 
engaging over 35 lakh persons. The sector engages over 25 lakh female weavers and 
allied workers which makes it an important source of economic empowerment of 
women. Handloom weaving constitutes one of the richest and most vibrant aspects 
of the Indian cultural heritage. The sector has advantage of being less capital 
intensive, minimal use of power, being eco-friendly, flexibility of small production, 
openness to innovations and adaptability to market requirements. Because of the 
uniqueness and exclusivity of designs, capability to produce small batch sizes and 
being eco-friendly fabric, handloom products are in high demand in the 
international and the domestic market and retailers with discerning clientele looking 
for reliable source of authentic handloom products on regular basis. 
 
5.2 One of the largest in terms of employment potential, Handloom industry, with 
28.23 lakh handlooms, plays a very important role in the country’s economy, 
producing both for domestic as well as international consumption. 
 
5.3 The major handloom export centers are Karur, Panipat, Varanasi & Kannur 
where handloom products like Bed linen, Table linen, Kitchen linen, Toilet linen, 
Floor coverings, embroidered textile materials, curtains etc. are produced for export 
markets.  
 
5.4 The Handloom industry mainly exports fabrics, bed linen, table linen, toilet 
and kitchen linen, towels, curtains, cushions and pads, tapestries and upholstery’s, 
carpets, floor coverings, etc. The major importing countries of Handloom products 
from India are USA, UK, Germany, Italy, France, Japan, Saudi Arabia, Australia, 
Netherland and UAE.

(a) National  Handloom Development Programme (NHDP) 
 
5.17 National Handloom Development Programme (NHDP) includes following 
Schemes/Programmes: 
 
(i) Small Cluster Development Programme (SCDP): Financial assistance upto 
₹ 2.00 crore per SCDP for various interventions such as Hathkargha 

36 
 
Samvardhan Sahayata, product development, construction of workshed, 
project management cost, design development etc. is provided. The 
proposals are recommended by the State Government. 
 
(ii) Handloom Marketing Assistance (HMA) is one of the components of 
National Handloom Development Programme.  In order to provide 
marketing platform to the handloom agencies/weavers to sell their 
products directly to the consumers, financial assistance is provided to the 
States/eligible handloom agencies for organizing marketing events in 
domestic as well as overseas markets.   
 
(iii) Special Infrastructure Projects: Objective of the scheme is to set up 
project/s for product development/diversification, improving the 
productivity/ quality of handloom products, value addition of handloom 
products, marketing etc. to meet challenges of the dynamic market. 
 
(iv) Mega Cluster Development Programme: Mega Handloom Clusters in 
various parts of the country will be taken up for their holistic 
development, drawing comprehensive development plans. Each Mega 
Handloom Cluster will cover atleast 10,000 handlooms with GoI 
contribution upto ₹ 30.00 crore per mega cluster. Nature and level of 
assistance to each Mega Cluster will be need based. 
 
(v) Concessional Credit/Weavers’ MUDRA Loan: Under the Scheme, margin 
money assistance for individual weaver and Handloom Organizations; 
interest subvention and credit guarantee fees on loans for a period of 
three years are provided to handloom organizations only. MUDRA Portal 
has been developed in association with Punjab National Bank to cut down 
delay in disbursement of funds for margin money, interest subvention 
and credit guarantee fee. 
 
(vi) Handloom Weavers’ Welfare: Handloom Weavers’ Welfare is providing life, 
accidental and disability insurance coverage under the components 
Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), Pradhan Mantri 
Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) and Converged Mahatma Gandhi Bunkar 
Bima Yojana (MGBBY).This scheme also provides scholarship for higher 
education to handloom weavers/workers’ children (upto 2 children) and 
financial support for Awardee weavers above 60 years of age in indigent 
circumstances. 
 
(vii) Hathkargha Samvardhan Sahayata (HSS): HSS was introduced on  
01 December 2016 with an objective to provide looms/accessories to the 
weavers to enhance their earnings through improved productivity and 
quality of the handloom products. Under the scheme, 90% of the cost of 
loom/accessory is borne by the Government of India while remaining 10% 
is borne by the beneficiary. The Government of India’s share is released to 
the supplier through Central Nodal Agency. 

37 
 
 
(viii) “India Handloom” Brand- During the celebration of 7th August 2015 as 
National Handloom Day, ‘India Handloom’ Brand was launched for 
branding of high-quality handloom products to promote production of 
niche handloom products with high quality with zero defect and zero 
effect on environment.  Since the launch of “India Handloom” Brand, 
2,191 registrations have been issued under 184 product categories. 
Initiatives with various leading brands has been undertaken to bring out 
a separate range of handloom garments in their brand. 
 
 
(ix) Urban Haats are set up in the big towns/metropolitan cities to provide 
adequate direct marketing facilities to the craft persons/weavers and 
eliminate middle agencies.  37 such Urban Haats have been sanctioned 
across the country so far, of which 35 Urban Haats are functional and 2 
are under process.  
 
(x) Producer Companies (PCs): Govt. of India is supporting in formation of 
PCs across the country in the handloom sector as a thrust area with the 
objective to extend the benefits of various handloom schemes to the 
weavers/workers, in particular to those who are either working 
independently or in the fold of Self-Help Groups/Producer Groups. 
Suitable handloom pockets have been identified and being facilitated for 
formation of Producer Companies for catering to the needs of the weavers 
and craftsmen there. So far, 163 PCs have been registered across the 
country.

VI. HANDICRAFTS SECTOR 
 
6.1 The handicrafts sector plays a significant role in the country’s economy. It 
provides employment to a vast segment of craft persons in rural & semi urban areas 
and serves as a pivotal driver of substantial foreign exchange earnings for the 
country, while concurrently preserving our rich cultural heritage. Handicrafts have 
great potential, as they hold the key for sustaining not only the livelihoods of 
millions of artisans spread over the length and breadth of the country, but also for 
the burgeoning number of newcomers entering in the crafts activity. 
 
6.2 Presently, handicrafts sector contributes substantially to employment 
generation and exports earnings. Despite its significant contribution to the economy, 
the sector faces myriad challenges stemming from its predominantly unorganized 
structure. Key constraints such as lack of education, inadequate capital resources, 

43 
 
insufficient exposure to modern technologies, a dearth of market intelligence, and 
the absence of a robust institutional framework hampered its growth potential. 
 
6.3 Total 33.55 lakh artisans have been mobilized under “Pahchan” initiative by 
the office of Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), Ministry of Textiles as on 
30.11.2025. 
 
6.4 The Office of Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) oversees the 
implementation of two pivotal schemes for promotion and development of 
handicrafts sector namely “National Handicraft Development Program” (NHDP) and 
Comprehensive Handicrafts Cluster Development Scheme (CHCDS) which has an 
integrated approach for development of handicraft clusters in a holistic manner. 
 
(I) National Handicrafts Development Program Scheme’s Components:  
 
a. Marketing Support & Services.  
b. Skill Development in Handicrafts Sector  
c. Ambedkar Hastshilp Vikas Yojana

VIII. SERICULTURE SECTOR 
 
8.1      Silk is an insect fibre, with lustre, drape and strength. Because of these 
unique features, silk is known as the “Queen of Textiles” the world over. India has 
been the land of ancient civilisation and has contributed many things to the world, 
silk being one of them. India is the second largest producer of silk in the world and 
also the largest consumer. Nevertheless, India is the only country, which is 
producing all the four commercial varieties of silk, namely Mulberry, Tropical & Oak 
Tasar, Muga and Eri. Indian sericulture industry has the unique distinction of high 
employment potential, low capital requirement and provides remunerative income to 
silk growers. India with the production of 38,913 MTs of silk is the second largest 
producer of silk in the world after China.  
      Among the four varieties of silk produced, Mulberry accounted for 76.82% 
(29,892 MT), Tasar 4.08% (1,586 MT), Eri 18.46% (7,183 MT) and Muga 0.65% (252 
MT). The bivoltine raw silk production has increased by 8.66% to 9,675 MT during 
2023-24 from 8,904 MT during 2022-23. Further, vanya silk, which includes Tasar, 
Eri and Muga silks, have increased by 1.04% during 2023-24 over 2022-23.

8.5  On being asked by the Committee as to what extent the Sericulture Industry in 
India is at par with its counterparts across the world, the Ministry submitted in their 
reply as under: 
 
   “India’s sericulture industry is broadly at par with leading global counterparts and 
holds a strategically strong position in the global silk economy. India is the second-
largest producer of raw silk in the world, next only to China, contributing about 42% 
(41,121 MT in 2024–25) of the global raw silk production (97,351 MT in 2024). 
Together, China and India account for nearly 95% of total global silk production, 
while production growth in other silk-producing countries remains limited. 
Significantly, India is the only country in the world that produces all four commercial 
varieties of silk—Mulberry, Tasar, Eri and Muga, reflecting its unique biodiversity and 
diversified production base.

education, training and input support systems, supported by indigenously developed 
advanced technologies across the silk value chain—from seed to fabric. With robust 
infrastructure, policy support and skilled manpower, India has substantial potential 
to further enhance domestic silk production, improve productivity and strengthen its 
global competitiveness. Additionally, India collaborates with technologically advanced 
sericulture nations to promote innovation, technology exchange and sustainable 
growth of the Indian silk industry.”

XI. PM MEGA INTEGRATED TEXTILE REGION & APPAREL (PM-MITRA) 
PARKS 
 
11.1 Ministry of Textiles had launched PM Mega Integrated Textile Regions and 
Apparel Parks (MITRAs) Scheme in October 2021 to strengthen the Indian textile 
industry by way of enabling scale of operations, reduce logistics cost by housing 
entire value chain at one location, attract investment, generate employment and 
augment export potential. The scheme is intended to develop integrated large scale 
and modern industrial infrastructure facility for total value-chain of the textile 
industry, for example, spinning, weaving, processing, garmenting, textile 
manufacturing, processing & printing machinery industry. These parks were 
envisaged to be located at sites which have inherent strengths for textile industry to 
flourish and have necessary linkages to succeed. The scheme envisaged leveraging 
Public Private Partnership model for fast paced implementation in a time-bound 
manner. 
 
So far, the Government has approved setting up of 7 (Seven) PM Mega Integrated 
Textile Region and Apparel (PM MITRA) Parks in Greenfield/Brownfield sites with 
world class infrastructure including plug and play facility with an outlay of Rs. 4445 
cr for a period of seven years upto 2027-28. 
 
The Government has finalised 7 sites viz. Tamil Nadu (Virudhnagar), Telangana 
(Warangal), Gujarat (Navsari), Karnataka (Kalaburagi), Madhya Pradesh (Dhar), 
Uttar Pradesh (Lucknow) and Maharashtra (Amravati) for setting up PM MITRA 
Parks.

implementation framework comprising a two-year gestation period during FY 2022–
23 and FY 2023–24, followed by five performance years from FY 2024–25 to FY 2028–
29. The Scheme appropriately provides adequate time for participating companies to 
operationalize investments, establish capacities, and stabilize production before 
becoming eligible to claim incentives based on incremental turnover. 
  
The initial pace of implementation was moderated by the lingering impact of the 
COVID-19 pandemic, which affected global supply chains, capital expenditure cycles, 
and project execution timelines. In addition, the prevailing global economic 
uncertainties, demand contraction in key export markets, and evolving trade 
measures, including tariff-related developments in the United States market, had a 
bearing on the pace of capacity expansion and scaling up of production in the initial 
years.

disbursement is expected to gain momentum in FY 2026–27 and progressively 
increase in subsequent years, in line with the ramp-up in production and 
incremental sales.

of applications, with substantial committed investments, capacity creation, and 
employment generation underway. With improving global demand conditions and 
stabilization of supply chains, the performance trajectory of participating companies 
is expected to strengthen in the coming years.

momentum during the performance period, leading to optimal and timely utilization 
of the total approved outlay of the Scheme.”

PART – II 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
GENERAL OVERVIEW  
1. PM Mega Integrated Textile Region & Apparel (PM-MITRA) Parks is the 
flagship programme of the Union Government and the Prime Minister to 
encourage development of Textiles sector which is the highest employment 
generation arena in the country. Hence, these Parks have been envisaged by 
the Government by investing a huge amount. These parks also boost the 
exports and economy of the nation. However, the Committee feel that the 
intent of the Union Government can be converted into a reality only with the 
coordination of all the State Governments, which is not forthcoming. 
Therefore, Union Government is urged to take concrete and concerted steps to 
effectively and successfully implement the above ambitious plan of the Prime 
Minister. 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION AND UTILISATION 
2. The Budgetary Allocation of the Ministry of Textiles was ₹ 4417.03 crore 
during FY 2024-25 which was revised downward to ₹ 3342.00 crore at the RE 
stage. The Actual Expenditure could reach only 89.72% of RE i.e. ₹ 2998.42 
crore. In the current FY 2025-26, budgetary allocation to the tune of ₹ 5272.00 
crore was enhanced at RE Stage to ₹ 5766.68 crore but the Actual Expenditure 
was only ₹ 3231.11 crore (as on 24.02.2026) which comprises 52% of the RE. 
The Committee are dismayed over the trend of under-utilization of earmarked 
funds in the previous years and the current fiscal. The funds to be utilized in 

90 
 
the current FY and that too in a period of one month is around 48% of the RE. 
The Ministry have assured the Committee that they are making concerted 
efforts to ensure optimal utilization of the allocated funds. 
 An amount of ₹ 1718.00 crore had been sought by the Ministry for 
disbursal of subsidy under payment of MSP which is still under approval by the 
Cabinet. The Committee desire that the Ministry should make vigorous efforts 
to obtain the approval of the Cabinet and disburse the subsidy for payment of 
MSP under the Central Sector Scheme for Procurement of Cotton in the 
current FY itself. The Committee also expect the Ministry to honour their 
commitment and make all out efforts to utilize the RE allocation by the end of 
FY 2025-26. 
3. The Committee observe that there had been shortfall in utilization under 
mainly five areas viz. Amended Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (ATUFS), 
National Handicrafts Development Programme, National Technical Textiles 
Mission (NTTM), Pradhan Mantri- Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel 
(PM-MITRA) and Cotton Corporation of India. The ATUFS was meant to 
incentivize modernization of textile industry with benchmark technologies 
with the objective to remove technological obsolescence in the textile 
industry. Despite the Scheme coming to an end on 31.03.2022, there had been 
allocation of funds under this Head continuously viz. ₹ 650.00 crore in 2022-
23, ₹ 675.00 crore in 2023-24 and ₹ 390.00 crore in 2024-25, for clearing the 
pending liabilities. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Scheme of 
ATUFS should continue as a separate Scheme and funds should be allocated 

91 
 
separately under the Head every year as the Scheme focuses on technology 
upgradation which is essential for improving efficiency, quality and 
competitiveness of the Textile Industry. 
4. The Committee note that the Ministry had submitted demands of  
₹ 13739.63 crore for FY 2026-27 which is quite high as compared to the 
demands of  ₹ 11053.00 crore in 2025-26. The Ministry attributed the higher 
demand towards ₹ 6615.00 crore sought for CCI for disbursal of subsidies to 
farmers to ensure payment of minimum support price and ₹ 635.00 crore 
sought for ATUFS. However, this demand was not accepted by the Ministry of 
Finance and only ₹ 5279.01 crore was allocated as BE 2026-27. The 
Committee, taking note of the fact that demands at BE stage have been 
slashed drastically to less than half, impress upon the Ministry to convincingly 
pursue the Ministry of Finance for grant of the funds sought at RE stage and 
Supplementary Grants stage. The Committee are of the view that the Ministry 
should have presented a convincing and justifiable proposal before the 
Expenditure Finance Committee so that the demands are not cut down and 
sufficient funds are allocated at the BE stage itself. As the RE provisioning is 
done during the beginning of last quarter of the FY, the Committee urge the 
Ministry to streamline budgetary planning process well in advance so that 
funds are not slashed at the BE stage. 
5. The Committee are of the considered view that the Ministry of Textiles 
play a crucial role in the growth and regulation of India’s textile and apparel 
sector which constitutes 2.3% of India’s GDP and provides employment to 

92 
 
approximately 4.5 crore workers. Its policies and initiatives directly influence 
manufacturing, trade, rural employment, and global competitiveness of the 
sector. The Committee, therefore, emphasise that the Ministry should enlarge 
its vision and mission, enhance its absorptive capacity and project adequate 
budgetary demands accordingly to justify its role in the trade and economy of 
the country. The Committee also urge the Ministry to strengthen its project 
planning and pipeline development, ensure clear implementation timelines and 
approval mechanisms to avoid delays in release of funds and utilization. They 
should also introduce advanced project preparation mechanisms and modify 
their vision and mission to put forth a compelling case for enhanced budgetary 
allocations to the Ministry of Finance at the BE stage itself. 
6. Scrutiny of the information provided by the Ministry indicates that there 
was surrender of savings to the tune of ₹ 1194.89 crore under revenue section 
and ₹ 1.17 crore under capital section during 2024-25. Though the Ministry 
have assured the Committee of full utilization of funds in the current FY  
2025-26, the Committee desire that the Ministry should make all possible 
efforts for realistic budgeting, proposing funds based on actual needs and 
proper monitoring of the ongoing projects by the programme divisions. The 
Committee also expect the Ministry to work diligently in the direction of 
improving administrative and procedural bottlenecks, strengthening 
coordination between the Ministry and State Governments and implementing 
agencies, issuing of strict timelines for providing Utilization Certificates, 
advanced preparation of proposals for the Schemes for upcoming years, etc. to 

93 
 
achieve the target of optimal utilization of the budgetary funds in the 
upcoming fiscal. 
7. The Committee note that the Ministry had to face challenges due to the 
cut in the proposed Demand for Grants at BE stage which has impacted launch 
of new Schemes/mission. The Ministry have informed the Committee that 
most of the Schemes under the 15th Finance Commission are likely to be 
completed by 31 March 2026 and the Ministry have come up with several new 
Schemes for the 16th Finance Commission cycle. The Committee are aware 
that dearth of budgetary allocation can significantly hinder the effective 
functioning of the Government by causing delay in implementation of Schemes 
and development programmes as well as lowering efficiency and productivity 
by creating administrative difficulties. The Committee, therefore, urge the 
Ministry to streamline its budgetary planning processes and come up with a 
foolproof mechanism to prioritize timelines, adopt technology and efficiency 
measures for gaining accuracy in expenditure projections, strengthen 
monitoring mechanism for strictly adhering to scheme-wise fund utilization 
and ensuring better co-ordination between Implementing Agencies/State 
Governments and the Ministry. A detailed proposal regarding budgetary 
requirement for new schemes for the 16th Finance Commission Cycle should be 
prepared well in advance and put forth to the Ministry of Finance for allocation 
of funds at RE stage. 
8. The Committee find that a total of 19 Audit C&AG/PAC Paras are pending 
as on 31 December 2025. Taking note of the fact that 14 out of 19 Audit Paras 

94 
 
are new paras and the draft replies of all the Audit paras are under approval of 
C&AG, the Committee desire that the status should be properly monitored for 
early settlement of all the pending audit paras. 
COTTON SECTOR 
9. The Committee note that under the Central Sector Scheme of 
Procurement of Cotton, ‘nil’ utilization has been indicated during FYs 2024-25 
and 2025-26. The Ministry have informed the Committee that the Expenditure 
Finance Committee recommended the total price support of ₹ 1718.56 crore (₹ 
1713 crore for 2023-24 and ₹ 5.56 crore as outstanding amount for FY 2022-
23) and the Cabinet Note in this regard is still under consideration which has 
resulted in ‘nil’ utilization of funds in the previous two FYs and the current FY. 
The Committee were further informed by the Ministry that after the approval 
of Cabinet Note, the entire amount would be disbursed before 31 March 2026. 
The Committee understand that the amount of ₹ 1718.56 crore is towards 
reimbursement purpose of previous years. For the current FY 2025-26, ₹ 0.01 
crore  has been allocated at BE stage. According to information provided by the 
Ministry, an amount of ₹ 6615.00 crore proposed by the Ministry in their 
Annual Plan 2026-27 would be available to the Ministry only at the RE stage, 
i.e., in the last quarter of FY 2026-27. The Committee are concerned over the 
non-allocation of procurement figures year after year at BE stage and direct 
the Ministry to pursue the concerned State Governments so that the 
requirement of funds for cotton procurement is received timely. As timely 
sanction of price support is imperative to reduce MSP related financial burdens 

95 
 
on the Government by minimizing interest costs on outstanding funds, the 
Committee desire that the Ministry should maintain close coordination with 
Cotton growing States and prepare proposal for release of price support well in 
advance for timely approval by the CCEA.  
10. The Committee are concerned to note that the superior quality extra-
long staple cotton is not produced or grown in large quantities in the country 
resulting in huge imports to meet the demand of local and international 
markets. The Committee understand that the Ministry of Agriculture have 
undertaken several initiatives to enhance the productivity of this variety to 
meet future demands. However, the Committee strongly feel that the Ministry 
of Textiles should take proactive measures to initiate proper research and 
development on their own, to come up with a solution so that farmers across 
the country could grow the highest quality of cotton. The Committee believe 
that farmers would be able to access better markets, gain higher rates and have 
improved profits through better yields from the extra long staple cotton. This 
would prevent them from to switching over to other crops for more profits and 
have a positive impact on bringing down the imports and expanding trade. The 
Committee desire that the Ministry of Textiles, without further delay, should 
make efforts in tandem with the State Governments and the Ministry of 
Agriculture & Farmers Welfare to come up with a proper solution to increase 
the cultivation area as well as enhance the quality of Indian cotton to ‘extra 
long staple cotton’. 

96 
 
 
HANDLOOM SECTOR 
11. The Handloom sector represents one of the largest unorganised economic 
activities of India. It constitutes an integral part of the rural and semi rural 
livelihood engaging over 35 lakh persons with 25,00,000 female workers and 
allied workers making it an important source of economic empowerment of 
women. The sector has an advantage of being less capital intensive, minimum 
use of power, being eco-friendly, flexibility of small production, openness to 
innovations and adaptability to market requirements. The Committee find that 
BE 2025-26 of ₹ 397.99 crore had been increased to  
₹ 434.84 crore at the RE Stage and out of it, only ₹ 361.13 crore has been 
utilised till 31 December 2025. The Ministry have assured that the earmarked 
funds would be fully utilised by the end of FY 2025-26. The Committee, 
nevertheless, desire that the Ministry should institutionalise quarterly 
financial review under the Handloom sector so that the funds are properly and 
evenly distributed and utilised in every quarter and there are no savings and 
surrendering of funds at the end of the financial year.  
12. The Committee observe that the National Handloom Development 
Programme (NHDP) and comprises of ten schemes, including Small Cluster 
Development Programme, Handloom Marketing Assistance, Special 
Infrastructure Projects, Handloom Weavers Welfare, Concessional 
Credit/Weaver’s MUDRA Loan Scheme, etc. The Committee understand that 
Concept Note for proposed draft EFC for 2026-27 to 2030-31 is under approval 

97 
 
of Department of Expenditure and the proposed financial target for NHDP for 
2026-27 is ₹ 968 crore. Given the new initiatives proposed for all round 
development and growth of the Handloom Sector, the Committee direct the 
Ministry to pursue the Department of Expenditure for timely approval of the 
Concept Note so that adequate funds are available for implementation of 
Schemes for the welfare of Handloom weavers and growth and development of 
the Handloom sector. 
 13.  The Committee observe that there are 3 clusters have been indentified 
under Handloom Sector which have been identified and an amount of ₹ 87.52 
crore has been released to them during 2025-26 up to 31 December 2025. The 
Committee believe that there are several other natural clusters which are very 
old and traditional and have been formed because of the legacy of trade 
occupancy and tradition. These are mostly located in the Southern States of 
Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and also in Odisha. The 
Committee are of the view that such clusters should be developed and 
accordingly direct the Ministry to make concerted efforts to identify them and 
assist them with the latest technology, infrastructure upgradation and 
marketing links. 
14. The Committee note that under the Concessional Credit/Weavers’ MUDRA 
Loan Scheme of NHDP, the target set for the financial year 2025-26 was to 
cover 0.25 lakh weavers but the achievement is only 0.052 lakh beneficiaries 
as on 31 January 2026. The reason for shortfall in achieving the targets was 
attributed to the fact that weavers MUDRA loan and other insurance schemes 

98 
 
are voluntary and lack of interest shown by the weavers is the major challenge 
faced by the Ministry in achieving the physical and financial targets. The 
Committee are of the considered view that the measures taken by the Ministry 
in this regard are not sufficient and emphasize the need to intensify awareness 
campaigns at the grassroots level by organizing regular awareness camps, 
chaupals, and cluster-level meetings in major handloom clusters. These 
activities should be conducted in collaboration with State Handloom 
Departments, banks, and local weaver societies to ensure that handloom 
weavers are fully informed about the benefits and procedures of the schemes. 
Further, the Ministry should arrange capacity-building programmes and 
training sessions for weavers through Weavers’ Service Centres (WSCs) and 
State agencies to improve technological and financial literacy. Dedicated 
facilitation support may also be provided to assist weavers in filling 
applications and completing required documentation. The Committee desire 
that Banks should be encouraged to participate in special credit camps in 
handloom clusters to facilitate on-the-spot processing of Weaver MUDRA loan 
applications. The Ministry should take initiative and coordinate with financial 
institutions to simplify documentation requirements and reduce delays in loan 
sanctioning so that the Scheme could benefit more and more weavers. 
HANDICRAFTS SECTOR 
15. The Handicrafts Sector plays a significant role in the country’s economy. 
Presently, handicrafts sector contributes substantially to employment 
generation and exports earnings. It provides employment to a vast segment of 

99 
 
craft persons in rural & semi urban areas and serves as a pivotal driver of 
substantial foreign exchange earnings for the country, while concurrently 
preserving our rich cultural heritage. The Committee note that in FY 2025-26, 
₹ 235.51 crore has been utilized till 12.02.2026 against the RE of ₹ 274.00 
crore. The Committee express their concern over the underutilization of funds 
and urge the Ministry to make all concerted efforts to process and settle all 
pending reimbursement claims and bills before the end of the financial year to 
ensure full utilisation of the allocated funds. The Office of the Development 
Commissioner (Handicrafts) should strengthen its monitoring mechanism by 
conducting regular review meetings with programme divisions and 
implementing agencies to track expenditure and resolve bottlenecks in fund 
utilization. In addition, the Ministry should maintain close coordination with 
implementing agencies to ensure timely submission of utilisation certificates, 
claims, and project reports, thereby facilitating faster release and utilization of 
funds. The Committee also desire that the Ministry should prepare a time-
bound action plan for the remaining period of the financial year to ensure that 
the balance funds are effectively utilized in line with the objectives of the 
schemes.  
16.  The Committee take note of the decreasing trend in the number of 
beneficiaries covered under NHDP under Handicrafts Sector. There are 
1,20,886 beneficiaries covered in 2022-23, 1,06,288 in 2023-24, 1,02,604 in 
2024-25 and only 77545 in 2025-26 up to 31 December 2025. The Committee 
express concern over the decrease in the number of beneficiaries and direct 
the Ministry to take necessary measures to expand the outreach and 

100 
 
implementation of the Programme so as to cover larger number of 
beneficiaries. Towards this end, the Ministry should strengthen awareness 
activities, enhance coordination with State Governments and Implementing 
Agencies, and simplify the application and approval processes. The Ministry 
should also ensure wider dissemination of information about the scheme and 
encourage greater participation from eligible beneficiaries, particularly in 
extreme rural and remote clusters, to maximize the overall impact of the 
scheme. 
WOOL SECTOR 
17. The Committee note that the Integrated Wool Development Programme 
(IWDP) is a major Scheme run by the Ministry of Textiles for the holistic 
growth of the Wool Sector. The objective of the IWDP scheme is to position 
India as a competitive and a quality manufacturer\supplier of woollen products 
through technological interventions and optimizing the different segments of 
the wool sector. Upon scrutiny of the details of the financial outlay under the 
Wool Sector, the Committee find that during 2024-25, BE was slashed from  
₹ 20.00 crore to ₹ 15.00 crore at RE Stage, while the AE was only ₹ 12.98 crore. 
During the current FY 2025-26, the RE was raised to ₹ 25.80 crore vis-à-vis BE 
of ₹ 18.28 crore while the AE was ₹ 14.92 crore (up to 31 December 2025). The 
reasons cited for the hike in RE 2025-26 was demands of funds for ongoing and 
newly sanctioned projects in the current FY. The Committee express concern 
over the persistent trend of underutilization of funds under the wool sector. 
The reasons cited by the Ministry include, slow implementation by the 

101 
 
State/UT Governments and Implementation Agencies; harsh climatic condition 
and closure of the roads for nearly six months resulting in delay in 
implementation of the projects under Pashmina Wool Development Scheme, 
etc. The Committee are not satisfied with the reasons put forth by the Ministry 
and impress upon the Ministry and the Central Wool Development Board 
(CWDB) to take immediate and appropriate steps to strengthen coordination 
with State/UT Governments and their Implementing Agencies to ensure timely 
execution of projects and improved fund utilisation under the wool sector 
schemes. A time-bound implementation plan should be prepared for all ongoing 
projects with clearly defined milestones and periodic progress reviews to 
ensure their completion within the stipulated timeframe. The Committee 
recommend that regular review meetings and monitoring mechanisms be 
institutionalised at the Ministry and at the Central Wool Development 
Board (CWDB) level to closely track the progress of projects and promptly 
address implementation bottlenecks. Considering the unique challenges under 
the Pashmina Wool Development Scheme in the Ladakh region, the Committee 
recommend adopting a special implementation strategy, including advance 
planning of activities during the accessible months and timely release of funds 
and materials before the winter season. Steps should be taken to provide 
training, technical guidance, and improved project management support to the 
State Implementing Agencies to strengthen their capacity to accelerate project 
execution. 
  

102 
 
SERICULTURE SECTOR 
18. India is the second largest producer of silk globally next to China. The total 
raw silk production in the country has registered an increase of 21.76% from 
33,770 MT in 2020-21 to 41,121 MT in 2024-25. During 2025-26, production 
of raw silk has reached 32,017 MT (up to December) and is expected to achieve 
42,300 MT by the end of the financial year. The value of Indian silk exports 
has also grown from ₹ 1773.38 crore during 2022-23 to ₹ 2582.29 crore in 
2025-26 (April to December-Provisional) while imports stood at ₹ 1456.18 crore 
during the same period. Though the volume of raw silk production and the 
value of silk exports has increased over the past years, India is far behind 
China which accounts for roughly 75% of the global raw silk production and 
hold dominance over the export market. India, however, occupies a unique 
position in the world as the only country to produce all the four commercial 
types namely, Mulberry, Eri, Tasar and Muga. The Indian sericulture industry 
is also an employment-oriented sector generating estimated employment to 
97.30 lakh persons during 2024-25.  
Given the diverse range of jobs and high employment potential offered by this 
sector in rural areas, especially for small and marginal farmers, women and 
marginalized communities and in view of the low capital requirement, the 
Committee call for a multi-pronged approach for growth and development of 
the sericulture sector. The Committee, therefore, recommend that a roadmap 
for the next five years be prepared for boosting the production of high quality 
silk and silk products through research in genetic improvement and breeding 

103 
 
of silkworms, technological upgradation in processing, product diversification, 
skill development of weavers and artisans, strengthening of international 
marketing for silk products, boosting exports and reducing reliance on imports 
of raw silk, etc.  Sericulture sector being vital for rural economic development, 
the Committee further recommend that the Government should leverage its 
unique position as the only country to produce all the four commercial types 
namely, Mulberry, Eri, Tasar and Muga to boost exports and an outcome-
oriented action plan be worked out annually commencing from FY 2026-27  
and the progress in this regard be intimated to the Committee. 
JUTE SECTOR 
19. India is the largest producer of raw jute in the world, producing 80.36 lakh 
bales to 91 lakh bales in 2025-26 as per First Production Estimates of Ministry 
of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare. The Jute industry is one of the major 
industries in the eastern region, providing direct employment to 0.37 million 
workers in organized mills and in diversified units including tertiary sector and 
allied activities and supports the livelihood of 4.0 million farm families. In 
addition, a large number of persons are engaged in the trade of jute. The 
Committee note that RE was reduced to ₹ 107.10 crore against BE of ₹ 128.00 
crore during 2025-26, yet the AE was ₹ 86.71 crore (as on 31.12.2025). The 
Committee are aware that the Jute Sector plays a significant role in the 
country’s sustainable economic development by providing employment, 
supporting rural livelihoods and contributing to exports. They are, therefore, of 
the considered view that the funds allocated for the growth and development 

104 
 
of this sector should not be surrendered as savings at the end of the FY. The 
Committee recommend that the Ministry should  develop a robust mechanism 
to ensure timely submission of claim applications by scheme beneficiaries so 
that funds can be released and utilized in a more balanced manner throughout 
the financial year rather than being concentrated in the last quarter. For this 
purpose, a strong monitoring and review mechanism should be developed to 
track the progress of financial and physical performance of the schemes on a 
quarterly basis and timely corrective actions taken, wherever necessary. In 
view of the delay in workforce recruitment in the Jute Corporation of India 
(JCI), the Committee recommend that the Ministry should expedite 
recruitment and strengthen institutional capacity to ensure smooth 
implementation of schemes and efficient utilization of allocated funds. 
20. Scrutiny of the figures related to physical and financial targets and 
achievements under the Capital Subsidy for Acquisition of Plant & Machinery 
(CSAPM) for Jute Diversified Products under National Jute Development 
Program (NJDP), to facilitate modernisation/upgradation of the existing Jute 
mills and MSME JDP Units reveals non-achievement of both the targets in the 
last three years as well as the current FY i.e. 2025-26. The Committee, 
therefore, urge the Ministry to conduct a detailed assessment to identify the 
key constraints faced by mills and MSME units in availing the subsidy, 
including financial constraints, procedural delays, or lack of technical 
awareness, and take corrective measures accordingly. The Committee 
recommend that the Ministry should undertake intensive awareness and 
outreach programmes among jute mills and MSME Jute Diversified Product 

105 
 
(JDP) units to ensure that potential beneficiaries are well informed about the 
benefits and procedures of the scheme. The Ministry should also work to 
simplify the application, documentation, and approval procedures under the 
scheme so as to encourage greater participation from eligible units, 
particularly MSMEs. The Committee desire that the Ministry should provide 
technical guidance and handholding support to MSME JDP units for project 
preparation, machinery selection, and submission of proposals to improve 
participation under the scheme.   
TEXTILES SECTOR 
PM MEGA INTEGRATED TEXTILE REGION & APPAREL (PM-MITRA) PARKS 
 
21. The Committee note that Ministry of Textiles have launched PM Mega 
Integrated Textile Regions and Apparel (PM MITRA) Parks Scheme in October 
2021 to strengthen the Indian textile industry by way of enabling scale of 
operations, reduce logistics cost by housing entire value chain at one location, 
attract investment, generate employment and augment export potential. The 
scheme will develop integrated large scale and modern industrial infrastructure 
facility for total value-chain of the textile industry, for example, spinning, 
weaving, processing, garmenting, textile manufacturing, processing & printing 
machinery industry. The Scheme has an outlay of ₹ 4445 crore for a period of 
seven years upto 2027-28.  
Scrutiny of details of financial outlay reveals that despite BE allocation 
of ₹ 300 crore each in the FYs 2024-25 and 2025-26, RE has been drastically 
cut down to ₹ 44.00 crore in 2024-25 and ₹ 200.00 crore in 2025-26. AE in 

106 
 
2024-25 was reported as ₹ 24.51 crore and in 2025-26, it was to the tune of  
₹ 162.66 crore (up to 31.12.2025). The Committee are concerned to note that 
fund utilisation was constrained as funds could only be released after the 
incorporation of Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) and the appointment of 
Master Developers. While SPVs have now been incorporated in all five 
Greenfield States, the Committee recommend that the Ministry should ensure 
strict timelines for operationalisation of SPVs in all PM MITRA Parks so that 
administrative delays do not hinder timely utilisation of allocated funds in 
future. As the appointment of Master Developers is a crucial prerequisite for 
implementation of the scheme, the Committee emphasize the need for 
establishing a time-bound and transparent mechanism for selection of Master 
Developers, with clearly defined milestones and accountability, to avoid delays 
in project execution and fund utilisation. The Committee also call for 
strengthening and maintaining close coordination between the Centre, States 
involved and the Implementing Agencies. Taking note of the fact that ₹164.17 
crore has been released and that steps are being taken to utilise the entire 
amount provided in the Revised Estimates during the current financial year, 
the Committee urge the Ministry to closely monitor the utilisation of RE 
allocation to ensure that the budgetary provision do not remain underutilized 
in the current FY.  
22. The Committee note that the Government has finalized 7 (seven) sites for 
PM MITRA Parks viz. Tamil Nadu (Virudhnagar), Telangana (Warangal), Gujarat 
(Navsari), Karnataka (Kalaburgi), Madhya Pradesh (Dhar), Uttar Pradesh 
(Lucknow) and Maharashtra (Amravati). However, all the 7 parks are still not 

107 
 
fully functional and some of them are still at the construction stage. In respect 
of Karnataka, the project is still at a preliminary stage, with processes such as 
finalisation of the Detailed Project Report, operationalisation of the Special 
Purpose Vehicle, and appointment of the Master Developer yet to translate into 
substantive progress on the ground. The Committee believe that the PM MITRA 
Parks proposed including in Kalaburgi, Karnataka would play a significant role 
in promoting integrated textile manufacturing and generating employment in 
the region, and are of the considered view that delays in the commencement of 
physical infrastructure development may adversely affect the timely 
achievement of the objectives envisaged under the PM MITRA Scheme. The 
Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of Textiles should take 
proactive measures, in close coordination with the State Governments 
concerned and the implementing agencies to expedite the pending procedural 
and implementation processes so as to ensure early commencement and time-
bound completion of the PM MITRA Parks including the proposed park at 
Kalaburgi. The Committee further recommend that the Ministry should pursue 
the DoE, Ministry of Finance to allocate enhanced budget provision for the 
early completion of the stuck-up projects of PM MITRA Parks as they are very 
ambitious programme of the Government of India where sustainable growth 
linked to exports is a key factor.  
PRODUCTION LINKED INCENTIVE (PLI) SCHEME FOR TEXTILES 
23. The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Textiles, with an 
approved outlay of ₹ 10,683 crore over a five-year period aims to promote 

108 
 
production of MMF Apparel, MMF Fabrics and Products of Technical Textiles in 
the country to enable Textile sector to achieve size and scale and become 
competitive. The Committee are concerned to note the extremely low 
utilisation of funds under the scheme during FY 2025–26, with only ₹ 16.58 
crore utilised against the Revised Estimate of ₹ 400.00 crore. The Ministry 
have apprised the Committee that disbursement of incentives is contingent 
upon eligible companies submitting claims after achieving the prescribed 
thresholds of investment, turnover, incremental turnover and value addition, 
and that such claims are to be filed by 31st December of the subsequent 
financial year after due statutory audit and verification.  The Committee are 
not satisfied with the slow pace of the progress made under PLI Scheme. The 
Committee understand that the scheme is performance-linked in nature and 
that claims are processed only after fulfilment of the stipulated criteria. 
However, they are of the considered view that such a substantial gap between 
the allocated funds and the actual utilisation points to slow pace in achieving 
the prescribed performance benchmarks by participating companies. The 
Committee, therefore, urge the Ministry to strengthen its monitoring and 
facilitation mechanisms for monitoring the progress of participating 
companies to ensure that the intended objectives of the scheme are realised 
within the envisaged timeframe. The Committee also desire that the Ministry 
should undertake periodic reviews with participating companies to identify 
implementation bottlenecks and extend necessary guidance so as to ensure 
optimal utilisation of the budgetary allocations in the current fiscal and 

109 
 
ensuing financial years. The Committee desire to be apprised of the progress 
made in this regard.  
  Scheme for Capacity Building in Textile Sector - SAMARTH 
24.  The Committee note that the Scheme for Capacity Building in Textile 
Sector - SAMARTH, managed by the Ministry of Textiles, is a demand-driven, 
placement-oriented, and implemented primarily by industry or industry 
associations. Under the Scheme, over six lakh persons have been trained, out 
of which 4.52 lakh have been placed and around 88 per cent of them are 
women. SAMARTH Scheme was formed under the broad skilling framework 
adopted by Ministry of Skill Development & Entrepreneurship and 
operationalized by a robust digital platform linked with Aadhaar Enabled 
Biometric Attendance System (AEBAS) for ease of implementation and 
monitoring of training programme under the scheme. The skilling programme 
under the scheme is implemented through Implementing Partners (IPs) 
comprising Textile Industry/ Industry Associations, Central/State Government 
agencies and Sectoral Organizations of Ministry of Textiles.  
The Committee note that as on 31.12.2025, an amount of ₹ 207.47 crore 
had been utilised against the Revised Estimate of ₹ 260.00 crore which 
constitutes approximately 79.6% and is broadly aligned with the quarterly 
implementation progress. Albeit the progress reported by the Ministry, the 
Committee emphasize that sustained monitoring is essential to ensure that 
the pace of implementation does not slow down during the later stages of the 
financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of 

110 
 
Textiles closely monitor the achievement of training and placement targets 
under the scheme and ensure timely release and utilisation of funds linked to 
the prescribed milestones. The Ministry should also strengthen coordination 
with implementing partners to avoid any delays in training delivery and 
reporting of outcomes so that the allocated funds are fully utilised within the 
financial year and the objectives of the scheme are achieved. 
INTEGRATIVE TEXTILES PROGRAMME (ITP) 
25. As announced in the Budget Speech, a new Scheme of Integrative Textiles 
Programme (ITP) was launched with an allocation of ₹ 1500 crore as BE  
2026-27. The Scheme encompass five programmes which includes, the 
National Fibre Programme, Textile Expansion and Employment Programme, 
Text Econ for Sustainability, and the Integrated Handmade Programme, which 
is an integration of the Handloom and Handicraft Schemes in a more concerted 
manner. The Committee note that the Integrated Textile Programme has been 
designed to promote the holistic development of the textile sector by 
supporting infrastructure creation, capacity building, and technological 
upgradation across various segments of the textile value chain. While the 
scheme has the potential to significantly enhance the competitiveness and 
sustainability of the textile industry, the Committee are concerned that the 
allocation of funds is not commensurate with the scope of the Scheme. The 
Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should make efforts to 
seek more funds over and above ₹ 1500 crore allocation so far, from the 
Ministry of Finance for this programme to take off as it is a very ambitious 

111 
 
programme, encompassing the growth of the entire textile sector, right from 
farm to fashion.   
NATIONAL TECHNICAL TEXTILE MISSION (NTTM) 
26. The National Technical Textiles Mission is a mission-mode programme 
started to improve India’s standing in technical textiles, which is the fastest 
growing segment globally. Out of the ₹ 1,480 crore outlay for five years,  
₹ 1,000 crore has been earmarked for research and development, and the 
remaining amount is for trading and other components. The Committee note 
that the RE has been revised downwards to ₹ 300 crore against the BE of ₹ 370 
crore during 2025-26. The Ministry have utilized a good chunk of the RE i.e. 
around ₹ 283 crore by February 2026 which roughly constitutes 94 per cent.  
While the Committee appreciate the Ministry’s efforts in achieving a high level 
of utilisation of the revised allocation, they are concerned that the downward 
revision of funds at the RE stage may impact the overall pace of 
implementation and the achievement of the intended objectives of the 
programme. The Committee are of the considered opinion that accurate 
assessment of fund requirements at the budgeting stage is essential to ensure 
stability in programme implementation. The Committee, therefore, 
recommend that the Ministry of Textiles should undertake realistic planning 
and projection of fund requirements at the Budget Estimate stage so as to 
minimise substantial revisions at the RE stage. Concerted efforts should also 
be made to ensure timely implementation and efficient utilisation of allocated 

112 
 
funds so that the objectives of the mission are achieved in a planned and 
sustained manner.

I. INTRODUCTORY 
1. The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) 
continued its unwavering commitment towards strengthening India’s skilling 
and entrepreneurship ecosystem in the last year. The Ministry’s initiatives were 
aimed at not only expanding the reach and quality of skill development efforts 
but also ensuring deeper convergence across Ministries, sectors, and 
geographies and ensuring industrial alignment of training efforts. MSDE played 
a pivotal role in reinforcing the skilling narrative as an enabler of India’s 
demographic dividend, economic growth, and global competitiveness. Building 
on the foundation of a decade of the Skill India Mission, the Ministry ushered in 
a new phase of systemic transformation through convergence with flagship 
Government programmes, partnerships with industry and international 
stakeholders, enhancement of institutional capacities, and a strong focus on 
inclusivity and future-readiness.  
2. The National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (NPSDE), 
launched in 2015 by the Ministry, acknowledges the need for an effective 
roadmap for promotion of skilling and entrepreneurship as the key to a 
successful growth strategy. The Vision of the Policy is to create an ecosystem of 
employment by Skilling on a large Scale at Speed with high Standards and to 
promote a culture of innovation-based entrepreneurship which can generate 
wealth and employment so as to ensure Sustainable livelihoods for all citizens 
in the country.  
3. The Mission of NPSDE is to: 
i) Create a demand for skilling across the country; 
ii) Correct and align skilling with required competencies; 
iii) Connect the supply of skilled human resources with sectoral 
demands; 
iv) Certify and assess in alignment with global and national standards; 
and 
v) Catalyse an ecosystem wherein productive and innovative 
entrepreneurship germinates, sustains and grows leading to creation 
of a more dynamic entrepreneurial economy and more formal wage 
employment. 
 
4. The National Skill Development Mission (NSDM) was approved by the 
Union Cabinet in July 2015. The Mission seeks to Create an end-to-end 
implementation framework for skill development, which provides opportunities 
for life-long learning. This includes: incorporation of skilling in the school 
curriculum, providing opportunities for qualities long and short-term skill 

2 
 
training, by providing gainful employment and ensuring career progression that 
meets the aspirations of trainees.  
5. The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship is supported by 
its associated organizations like - the Directorate General of Training (DGT), 
National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET), and National 
Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) in its endeavour to foster seamless 
interaction and collaboration to overcome the challenges within India’s skilling 
and entrepreneurship landscape.  
6. An analysis of the financial and physical performance of the Ministry of 
Skill Development and Entrepreneurship and its Attached and Subordinate 
Organizations in the process of implementation of certain Schemes/Projects has 
been made in the Report.

10. The Committee observed that there has been a significant increase in the 
BE during 2024-25 (28.50%), 2025-26 (34.95%) and 2026-27 (62.05%) as 
compared to the previous year. However, the RE was scaled down with drastic 
reduction from Rs.6100.10 crore to Rs.2703.54 crore during FY 2025-26. When 
asked to state the reasons along with the schemes/projects to be taken up with 
the enhanced allocation and the pre-emptive measures proposed to ensure that 
the budgetary allocation for 2026-27 is not reduced at RE stage, the Ministry 
responded stated as under:-  
“Reason for increase in BE and low expenditure during F.Y. 2024-25. 
Budgetary allocation for the year 2024-25 was majorly increased by Rs.1000 crore over BE-2023-24 for the new Centrally Sponsored Scheme namely “New ITI Upgradation Scheme” announced in the Regular Budget of F.Y 2024-25 and additional funds of Rs.400 crore in ‘Skill India Programme(SIP)’.  
‘New ITI Upgradation Scheme’ - After announcement, the Scheme was formulated & appraised by EFC in the F.Y 2024-25, however, the Cabinet approved this Scheme only on 07.05.2025 Therefore, the projection under RE-2024-25 was curtailed. This scheme has now 

4 
 
been renamed as “Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs” (PM-SETU).  
‘Skill India Programme’ – In anticipation of the Cabinet approval of this scheme, budget estimates were projected on the basis of year-wise allocations recommended by the EFC. However, the scheme was approved by the Cabinet only on 07.02.2025. Meanwhile, expenditure had to be limited to the extent allowed by DoE from time to time. Department of Expenditure (DoE) did not allow MSDE to incur expenditure between October, 2024 to January, 2025. This adversely impacted the training and only after Cabinet approval in February, 2025, the Ministry was able to book expenditure in the last quarter.  F.Y. 2025-26 
PM-SETU Scheme - Budgetary allocation of MSDE have been majorly increased for the years 2025-26 and 2026-27 due to additional allocation of Rs.2000 crore and Rs.3140 crore respectively in the PM-SETU Scheme. In this Scheme, release of Central Government contribution is contingent upon approval of Strategic Investment Plans (SIPs), on-boarding of Anchor Industry Partners (AIPs), and subsequent formation of industry-led Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs). As this is a State-driven, proposal-based mechanism, States/UTs are required to invite relevant AIPs and finalize SIPs before funds can be utilized through SPVs. Since, as on date, no SIP has been finalized and the process remains in the preparatory stage with EOIs and RFPs under evaluation, allocations were rationalized and subsequently decreased at the RE-2025-26 stage.  The enhanced allocation for FY 2026-27 is justified as the PM-SETU project has now moved beyond the preparatory phase. With groundwork completed, States/UTs are expected to progress past the Expression of Interest/ Request for Proposal (EOI/RFP) stage into evaluation of proposals submitted by Anchor Industry Partners (AIPs). In addition, five NSTIs are envisaged to onboard Lead Industry Partners (LIPs). As Sectoral Implementation Plans (SIPs) are approved, expenditure will be driven by the formation of Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) under Component I and Industry Management Committees (IMCs) under Component II. This progression marks the transition from planning to execution; hence this progression justifies the enhanced allocation of Rs. 6140.50 crore for FY 2026-27.  Skill India Programme - Following the Cabinet approval and drawing upon the learnings from the previous financial years, the Ministry has taken several corrective measures in FY 2025–26 to strengthen quality, compliance, and robustness in implementation before allocation of targets. Key measures undertaken include: - i. Issuance of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to streamline the assessment and certification process.  ii. Revision of monitoring guidelines to strengthen oversight of 

5 
 
training delivery and ensure adherence to scheme norms.  iii. Rigorous scrutiny of proposals in compliance with extant guidelines prior to approval and target allocation.  Mandating face authentication and geo-tagged attendance for candidates, trainers, and assessors under PMKVY 4.0 to enhance transparency and monitoring.  iv. Strengthening monitoring and independent oversight through Kaushal Samiksha Kendras (KSK) enabling large-scale virtual and physical inspections, supplemented by regular field inspections by State and District coordinators. v. Initiation of strict disciplinary actions against non-compliant centres, including blacklisting, suspension of centres, stoppage of payments, issuance of Show Cause Notices, cancellation of Accreditation and Affiliation, and filing of FIRs, to deter future violations.  vi. Capturing candidate feedback through NIC’s Central Communication Layer (CCL).  To ensure optimal utilization of funds in FY 2025–26, the Ministry has undertaken concerted efforts to promote high-quality skill training through credible and well-established institutions including State Skill Development Missions (SSDMs), Institutes of National Importance (INIs), Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and other reputed organizations. The Ministry has also hosted a structured online application form with necessary validations on the Skill India Digital Hub (SIDH) to invite and process training proposals from industries / industry associations / SMEs, thereby strengthening industry participation and demand-driven skilling under the scheme.  
Integrated Scheme in Skilling Architecture – New Central Sector 
Scheme 
Initially total budget of the Ministry was Rs.9285.80 crore for the year 2026-27. Meanwhile, a new Central Sector Scheme namely “Integrated Scheme in Skilling Architecture” has been announced in the Regular Budget of F.Y 2026-27 with the total budget outlay of Rs.600 crore. This new scheme is under formulation. Consequently, total budget of the Ministry has been increased from Rs.9285.80 crore to Rs.9885.80 crore leading to 62.05% increment for F.Y 2026-27 as compared to last year’s budget”.

13. When the Committee enquired about the reasons for substantial shortfall 
in expenditure vis-à-vis the RE over the past three years and particularly in FY

that the entire allocation is utilized within the remaining period of 2025-26, the 
Ministry stated as under:         

8 
 
“The Ministry has been able to prudently utilize maximum funds in Establishment expenditure.  Skill India Program(SIP) is a composite Central Sector Scheme consisting of ‘Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana(PMKVY.4.0)’, Jan Shikshan Sansthan(JSS) and National Apprentice Promotion Scheme(NAPS). Expenditure in the two components viz., JSS and NAPS has been significant in the last three years and the same pace is maintained in current F.Y 2025-26.  Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) 4.0, as part of the Composite Central Sector scheme, Skill India Programme (SIP) was approved by the Cabinet on 07.02.2025 from FY 2022–23 onwards. Prior to this approval, the scheme was being implemented on the basis of phased approvals granted by the Department of Expenditure from time to time. This phase wise approval process led to slower progress and a substantial shortfall in expenditure.  Following the Cabinet approval and drawing upon the learnings from the previous financial years, the Ministry has taken several corrective measures in FY 2025–26 to strengthen quality, compliance, and robustness in implementation before allocation of targets. Key measures undertaken include:-  Issuance of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to streamline the assessment and certification process.   Revision of monitoring guidelines to strengthen oversight of training delivery and ensure adherence to scheme norms.   Rigorous scrutiny of proposals in compliance with extant guidelines prior to approval and target allocation.   Mandating face authentication and geo-tagged attendance for candidates, trainers, and assessors under PMKVY 4.0 to enhance transparency and monitoring.   Strengthening monitoring and independent oversight through Kaushal Samiksha Kendras (KSK) enabling large-scale virtual and physical inspections, supplemented by regular field inspections by State and District coordinators.  Initiation of strict disciplinary actions against non-compliant centres, including blacklisting, suspension of centres, stoppage of payments, issuance of Show Cause Notices, cancellation of Accreditation and Affiliation, and filing of FIRs, to deter future violations.   Capturing candidate feedback through NIC’s Central Communication Layer (CCL).

This scheme is ending with this F.Y 2025-26. 29. The Committee observed that under PMKVY.4.0, Demand driven skilling 
responding to national priorities and industry requirements contributing 
through skill gap studies and curriculum design, trainers, training 
infrastructure have been introduced. When asked about the response and 
outcome as compared to the earlier three versions, the Ministry submitted as 
below: -                                                                     
“There are significant structural and operational enhancements introduced 
under Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) 4.0 over earlier 
Scheme versions, aimed at improving relevance, industry alignment, 
governance, and outcomes. 
a) Shift from Supply-Driven to Demand-Driven Skilling:  
While earlier versions largely followed a top-down target allocation 
approach that occasionally led to training in job roles with limited local 
demand, PMKVY 4.0 adopts a demand-driven framework. Training 
proposals are now increasingly aligned with skill gap studies, sector-
specific and regional demand patterns and emerging future-ready job roles 
such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), Drone Technology, Robotics, Industry 
4.0, and Green Jobs. 
b) Rationalization of Scheme Components:  
Considering the lower participation of States under the Centrally Sponsored 
State Managed (CSSM) component in PMKVY 2.0 and 3.0, PMKVY 4.0 
retains only the Centrally Sponsored Centrally Managed (CSCM) 
component. However, States continue to play an active role by participating 
as Project Implementing Agencies (PIAs), enabling them to execute allocated 
targets.  
c) Integration of On-The-Job (OJT):  
PMKVY 4.0 incorporates an enhanced On-the-Job Training (OJT) 
component, providing candidates with practical, industry-based exposure 
that was limited in earlier Scheme phases.  
d) Emphasis on New-Age and Emerging Skill Areas: 
PMKVY 4.0 places strong emphasis on new-age job roles and advanced 
technologies, including Artificial Intelligence, Cyber Security, 
Semiconductors, and other emerging sectors aligned with national 
priorities.  
e) Strengthened Monitoring Framework: 
PMKVY 4.0 features a significantly strengthened monitoring mechanism, 
including face authentication, geo-tagged attendance, e-KYC for candidates 
and trainers, and stricter scrutiny of proposals and liabilities. These 
measures enhance transparency, accountability, and program integrity. 
f) Enhanced Collaboration with Premier Institutions: 

23 
 
PMKVY 4.0 encourages collaboration with Institutions of National 
Importance (INIs), including IITs, NITs, IIMs, etc. The Scheme leverages 
the advanced infrastructure of these institutions, including laboratories, 
specialized equipment, and expert trainers/ faculty for delivering high-
quality training programs to candidates. 
 
g) Industry Engagement: 
MSDE is actively and consistently engaging with private sector to 
strengthen the implementation of PMKVY 4.0. This collaborative approach 
aims not only to deliver high-quality skill training but also to facilitate 
employment and placement opportunities for certified candidates. To 
achieve this objective, MSDE has signed multiple MoUs with industry 
partners which includes Air India Sats Airport Services Private Ltd, 
Confederation of Indian Textile Industries (CITI), Simplex Infrastructure 
Ltd, Flipkart Internet Private Ltd, Swiggy Ltd, etc.”    
30. When further enquired how the training courses under PMKVY 4.0 are 
identified and prepared by District Skill Committees (DSCs) so as to meet the 
local industrial needs, the Ministry stated as under:  
“PMKVY 4.0 follows a demand-driven framework to ensure that training 
courses are aligned with local industrial requirements and evolving labour 
market needs. The identification and preparation of training courses involve 
a layered, evidence-based process integrating district, state, and national-
level input.  
District Skill Committees (DSCs) play a key role in assessing local skill 
requirements through the preparation of District Skill Development Plans 
(DSDPs). These plans capture district-specific data, including Local 
industry demand, Sectoral employment opportunities, availability of 
training infrastructure, etc. This ensures that skilling interventions are 
responsive to regional economic conditions. 
The district-level assessments are consolidated by the State Skill 
Development Missions (SSDMs) into State Skill Development Plans 
(SSDPs). Training proposals under PMKVY 4.0 are routed through SSDMs, 
thereby ensuring: alignment with district-level skill gaps, consistency with 
State-specific priorities and optimal allocation of training targets 
At the national level, MSDE conducts regular skill gap studies with 
sectoral and geographical focus. These studies incorporate inputs from: 
District Skill Development Plans (DSDPs), Industry consultations, Sectoral 
growth projections. This approach captures both current and emerging 
job market needs, particularly in high-growth sectors such as logistics, 
pharmaceuticals, electronics, and other priority industries, including those 
in Tier II and Tier III cities. 
To ensure market relevance, the formulation of job roles follows a stringent 
validation mechanism. As mandated by NCVET, Awarding Bodies are 
required to obtain validation of job roles from a minimum of 30 industry 

24 
 
partners prior to approval. This safeguards industry alignment, 
employment relevance and standardisation of qualifications.  
MSDE conducts industry consultation workshops to refine training design 
and delivery. Since May 2024, MSDE has conducted 13+ industry 
consultations, engaging 120+ industries across multiple sectors. Key 
industry participants include organisations such as Larsen & Toubro, 
Flipkart, Swiggy, CREDAI, etc.”

Some practical challenges have been encountered and constructively addressed. 
Many educational institutions and technical institutes were first-time 
implementers of PMKVY and needed hand-holding on mobilization, Aadhaar 
Enabled Biometric Attendance System (AEBAS), SIDH data entry, assessment 
protocols and financial norms. This has been mitigated through orientation 
workshops, standard operating procedures and dedicated support from NSDC 
and State Skill Development Missions. For certain future skill courses, the high 
initial costs associated with labs, software licenses, and specialized trainers 
made it difficult to deliver training at discounted Common Cost Norms (CCN) 
rates. Accordingly, the Steering Committee permitted the adoption of original 
CCN rates for select job roles and approved a 30 per cent advance to Government 
educational institutions to support upfront expenditure.  
32. The Committee perceive that under PMKVY 4.0, candidate feedback is 
captured during training lifecycle and whole lifecycle is captured through Skill 
India Digital Hub (SIDH) portal. When asked about the success level of the 
system as a monitoring mechanism of the implementation of PMKVY 4.0 and the 
improvements proposed to enhance the monitoring system through this digital 
platform, the Ministry stated as under: -  
 
“Under PMKVY 4.0, the Skill India Digital Hub (SIDH) serves as a 
comprehensive digital platform designed to enhance transparency, 
monitoring and quality assurance across the training lifecycle. The system 
has strengthened program oversight through structured data capture, real-
time tracking, and technology-enabled feedback mechanisms. 
SIDH incorporates an independent and systematic framework for capturing 
feedback at multiple stages of the training lifecycle. Key features include:  
a) Automated WhatsApp-based notifications to candidates and trainers 
b) Feedback collection at predefined milestones 
c) Systematic recording and analysis of responses 
This enables continuous assessment of training quality, learner 
experience, and overall programme effectiveness. 

26 
 
Apart from the candidate feedback collections, revised monitoring guidelines 
have been approved by MSDE as of December 2025. The summary of the key 
revisions incorporated to strengthen the scheme monitoring have been 
provided below: 
a) Comprehensive monitoring framework and data based automated 
monitoring system has been proposed. KPIs and monitoring 
checkpoints throughout the scheme lifecycle have been defined to 
ensure end to end scheme level monitoring.  
b) Penalty matrix has been revised to comprehensively list penalties that 
shall be levied on the Training Partner and Training Centre in case any 
non-compliance is observed during inspections and other monitoring 
mechanisms. The penalty matrix defines the first and subsequent 
penalties at the Training Centre and Training Partner level, for all 
possible non-compliance and frauds observed.  
c) Role of states in monitoring has been defined and strengthened to 
ensure decentralization and reinforcement of monitoring process 
d) The overall monitoring process has been defined, covering (but not 
limited to) central monitoring planning, physical inspection process and 
format, non-compliance identification and analysis, imposing penalty 
for confirmed non- compliance and appeals handling for aggrieved 
parties. 
e) Process and checklist for tranche wise pre- payment verification has 
been defined. 
f) Face Authentication (geo fenced) based attendance recording at all 
PMKVY centres has been mandated.  
g) Physical Inspection, Virtual Monitoring and candidate feedback formats 
to be used for monitoring have been defined. 
h) Live attendance dashboard has been developed on Skill India Digital 
Hub (SIDH) to provide insights into scheme level outputs and outcomes 
mapped with candidate lifecycle, training centre performance, and 
assessment outcomes, 
i) QR-coded digital certificates to ensure authenticity, facilitating instant 
verification and boosting employer confidence 
j) A structured online application form has been hosted on SIDH for 
shortlisting PIAs/TPs based on filtration criteria and priority sectors for 
allocation of targets to private organizations. 
The guidelines also outline the multi-pronged robust monitoring 
mechanism including - biometric attendance, CCTV-based monitoring, 
virtual verification, physical inspections, trainee feedback, and SIDH-based 
automated dashboard to be employed for real-time compliance tracking.”

regard to capturing Candidate Feedback during the Training Lifecycle through 
Central Communication Layer (CCL) developed by NIC and the status of 
capturing whole training lifecycle of the candidate through Skill India Digital

“MSDE has not received any formal feedback regarding mechanism for

34. On a query whether the existing training infrastructure in the country has 
been identified/mapped to ensure its optimal utilization under PMKVY 4.0 and 
the percentage utilization of such training infrastructure, the Ministry 
responded as follows:-                                               
“Under Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) 4.0, a demand-
driven framework has been adopted to ensure efficient and need-based 
utilization of training infrastructure across the country. Training Centres 
(TCs) are empaneled through a structured process of accreditation and 
affiliation at SIDH. TCs are affiliated based on infrastructure availability, 
training capacity, geographical location and alignment with sectoral skill 
demand, while ensuring compliance with prescribed quality norms. 
Under PMKVY 4.0, more than 15,000 Training Centres, including 
Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), Polytechnics, Skill Hubs, and Private 
Training Centres, have been identified, geo-tagged and mapped through 
SIDH. It is, however, clarified that the identification of 15,000+ Training 
Centres does not imply their simultaneous operation. The affiliation and 
activation of Training Centres is a continuous and dynamic process, with 
centres being operationalized based on target allocation to PIAs, sectoral 
requirements and regional demand. 
The utilization levels of Training Centres are dynamic in nature and vary 
across States, sectors and training cycles. Given the demand-driven and 
flexible operational framework, a fixed percentage of utilization is not 
maintained, as centre activation is contingent upon program requirements 
and market demand.”

is as under:

trainer competency skills. The curriculum comprises theory and practical 
components delivered through:

adult learning principles and pedagogy, competency-based and 
outcome-based training approaches, integration of employability 
skills, digital and blended learning methodologies, assessment and

Standards (NOS), including sector-specific tools, equipment and

quality and reach of the ToT ecosystem. Specialized institutes of national
