 HANDLOOM SECTOR 
7. The Committee note that the Handloom Sector is one of the largest 
unorganized economic activities of India and it constitutes an integral part of 
the rural and semi- rural livelihood engaging over 35 lakh persons. The sector 
engages over 25 lakh female weavers and allied workers. Handloom weaving 
constitutes one of the richest and most vibrant aspects of the Indian cultural 
heritage. The sector has advantage of being less capital intensive, minimal use 
of power, being eco-friendly, flexibility of small production, openness to 
innovations and adaptability to market requirements. One of the largest in 
terms of employment potential, Handloom industry, with 28.23 lakh 
handlooms, plays a very important role in the country’s economy, producing 
both for domestic as well as international consumption. The Committee find 
that there are several Schemes /programmes in the Handloom Sector for the 

 
80 
 
welfare of Handloom weavers.  Under this Sector, the Ministry have utilized  
₹ 337.56 crore out of RE of ₹ 378.01 crore during FY 2024-25 till January, 
2025. Albeit the Ministry have assured the Committee that the allocated funds 
will be fully utilized by the end of this FY, still the Committee desire that the 
Ministry should achieve the physical/financial targets under various schemes 
of the Sector, as stipulated. Further, the Committee are made aware that the 
Ministry are taking various measures to tackle the hurdles in the way of full 
utilization of earmarked budget such as requesting the State/UT Governments 
to submit the proposals in time, organizing meetings by the senior officers to 
review the progress with field officers as well as offices of State/UT 
Governments, etc. The Committee, nevertheless desire that the Ministry 
should also set up a reliable monitoring mechanism under the Financial 
Advisor to ensure that these steps taken by the Ministry actually work without 
fail and result in full utilization of allocated funds. 
8. The Committee, during the examination of previous year’s Demands for 
Grants (2024-25), had recommended making the enrolment of Handloom 
workers/artisans mandatory under PMJJBY/PMSBY under Handloom Weavers’ 
Welfare Scheme of NHDP. The Ministry have informed that the enrolment of 
handloom weavers/workers under PMJJBY & PMSBY has increased from 0.70 
lakh in policy year 2022-23 to 1.35 lakh in policy year 2023-24 and 1.33 lakh 
weavers in 2024-25 (up to 31.01.2025). The Committee also learn that State 
Directorates of Handlooms and its subordinate offices in the field are Nodal 
Agency for implementation of the Scheme. The Nodal Agency will act for and 
on behalf of the insured members in all matters relating to insurance cover. 

 
81 
 
The target fixed by the Government of India is also purely based on the targets 
indicated by the State Governments. As Office of DC (Handlooms) is 
responsible for implementing the welfare Schemes under Handloom Sector, the 
Committee urge the Ministry that Office of DC (Handlooms) should make more 
coordinated efforts with the State Directorate of Handlooms to spread 
awareness about these two insurance Schemes amongst the Handloom weavers. 
Though the Committee is appreciative of the efforts taken up by the Ministry 
as the number of beneficiaries are rising every year since 2022-23, it is felt 
that the Ministry have a long way to go as there are nearly 35 lakh weavers 
working under this sector and only around 3.38 lakh are covered in the last 
three years including 2024-25. As the aim is to cover more and more 
Handloom weavers under the insurance Schemes, therefore the Committee 
desire that the Ministry should establish proper coordination with the 
State/UT Governments to ensure better coverage of handloom weavers under 
these insurance Schemes.  
National Handloom Development Programme (NHDP) 
9. There are ten Schemes/programmes run under NHDP by the Ministry of 
Textiles such as Small Cluster Development Programme (SCDP), Handloom 
Marketing Assistance (HMA), Mega Cluster Development Programme, Handloom 
Weavers’ Welfare, etc. The Committee note that ₹ 189.49 crore had been 
utilized as on 25.02.2025 against the RE 2024-25 of ₹ 198.84 crore under 
NHDP. The Ministry are expecting full utilisation of RE amount in the current 

 
82 
 
fiscal. The Committee, therefore, hope that the Ministry would make concerted 
efforts and utilise the entire earmarked budget under this head.  
Concessional credit/weavers MUDRA Loans Scheme under NHDP 
10. National Handloom Development Programme (NHDP) comprises several 
Schemes/Programmes for the welfare of Handloom weavers. Concessional 
credit/weavers MUDRA Loans is one of these schemes covered under NHDP. 
The Committee note that the State-wise MUDRA loan details have been 
furnished by the Ministry, but the loan disbursement details regarding North 
Eastern States other than Manipur cannot be seen. Taking note of the above 
fact, the Committee recommend the Ministry to consider special provisions 
including relaxed eligibility parameters and shortened sanctioning procedure 
for the North East as the Mudra loan facility is a critical intervention for the 
economic and social upliftment of the Handloom weavers. 
HANDICRAFTS SECTOR 
 
11. The handicrafts sector plays a significant role in the country’s economy. It 
provides employment to a vast segment of craft persons in rural & semi urban 
areas and serves as a pivotal driver of substantial foreign exchange earnings for 
the country, while concurrently preserving our rich cultural heritage. The 
Committee are concerned to note that in FY 2024-25, only ₹ 137.68 crore were 
utilised till January, 2025 vis-à-vis RE of 206.80 crore which amounted to 
around 66 per cent which indicates that around 44 per cent of the allocated 
funds were to be utilised within the last quarter of the financial year under 
Handicrafts Sector. Also, under the Scheme of National Handicraft 

 
83 
 
Development Programme (NHDP), the utilisation was much less than expected 
i.e ₹ 108.94 crore out of RE of ₹ 175.00 crore till January, 2025. The Ministry 
attributed this delay in utilisation of funds to the mandatory transition from 
Central Nodal Agency (CNA) module for fund flow for Central Schemes (CS) and Central 
Sponsored Schemes (CSS) to the Treasury Single Account Module, which was under 
process during the first three quarters of FY 2024-25. Transition to TSA Module had 
taken time which could be fully implemented in the second week of December, 2024, 
causing delay in release of grants resulting in less utilisation of funds. The Committee 
find that this is one of the reasons repeated under many Schemes by the 
Ministry causing under-utilisation. The Committee opine that though it may be 
a better system of accounting, such procedural matters should have never 
come in the way of implementation of Schemes/Programmes of the 
Government. The Committee take strong exception to such avoidable reasons 
causing sub-optimal performance of schemes, especially those that are 
intended for weavers, artisans and handicraft sector that needs focussed 
handholding and recommend that causes of this nature should not be allowed 
to encumber the efficient implementation of schemes.  
12. The Committee are given to understand  that the major challenges faced by 
the Ministry in effectively implementing the Schemes/programmes under the 
Schemes of Handicrafts sector are non-receipt of timely and viable proposals 
from Implementing Agencies, non-submission of Utilization Certificates (UCs) 
and other documents by the implementing agencies on time, infrastructure 
projects delay in land acquisition by the implementing agencies, mandatory 
transition to Central Nodal Agency (CNA) and then Treasury Single Account 

 
84 
 
(TSA) module by the Central Ministries, etc. The Committee are not impressed 
to note the cliched and time worn answers about the problems faced by the 
Ministry in the implementation of Schemes under Handicraft Sector and 
measures taken to alleviate them. It is the firm opinion of the Committee that 
the Ministry shall take goal driven proactive measures to take feedback from 
the beneficiaries of these schemes and come up with effective provisions that 
bring results on the ground. 
WOOL SECTOR  
13. The Committee note that the primary reason for under-utilization of funds 
in previous years from 2021-24 is the slow progress in project execution by the 
State Government Implementing Agencies, particularly under the Pashmina 
Wool Development Scheme in Ladakh. Harsh climatic conditions and prolonged 
road blockages for 5-6 months have constrained the timely implementation of 
projects in this region.  Further, delay in submission of utilisation certificates 
under schemes have also hampered speedy utilization of funds. The 
Committee, taking note of the above fact, recommend that the Ministry should 
take up with the Ministry of Finance the aspect of harsh climatic conditions 
and terrain in areas like Ladakh hindering implementation of schemes of Wool 
Sector as they have to adhere to common expenditure guidelines relating to 
schemes.  Ministry of Finance be impressed upon the need for granting 
relaxation in spending limits and for putting in place tailor made provisions for 
schemes implemented in areas like Ladakh considering the uniqueness of the 
conditions on the ground where beneficiaries of the scheme reside.  

 
85 
 
14. Further, the Committee are of the considered opinion that the fact now 
Ladakh is a UT and not a State should allow more leverage to the Ministry of 
Textiles to take up the problem of slow progress in project execution by the UT 
Government Implementing Agencies, particularly under the Pashmina Wool 
Development Scheme in Ladakh. The Committee accordingly recommend that 
the Ministry of Textiles should take up this matter with the UT Government of 
Ladakh and if needed, with the Ministry of Home Affairs so that the wool 
producers are able to fully avail the benefits of the Scheme. 
15. The Committee note that CWDB has sanctioned a project to evaluate the 
current Wool Sector schemes implemented by various government agencies 
across different States. The Committee are of the view that Wool Sector needs 
special attention of the Government as it is interlinked with the contribution 
to the overall development of the Textile sector in the country as well as with 
the livelihood of wool-growers and artisans. Hence the Committee exhort that 
the evaluation and resultant revamping of the Wool sector Schemes shall be 
taken up on priority and completed expeditiously. Owing to the specificities of 
the sector and the regions where wool is produced in India, the Committee also 
impress upon the Ministry to undertake an effective ground level survey and 
other similar feedback as part of the review of the Schemes.     
SILK SECTOR 
16. The Committee note that to assess the impact of Silk Samagra-2 Scheme in 
the field and to suggest mid-course corrections / modification in the scheme 
implementation, a Mid-term evaluation study through a third party, is under 

 
86 
 
progress. The Committee are of the considered opinion that the revamping of 
the Scheme has to be completed on preferential basis and unique requirements 
of the silk producing areas like the North East shall be taken into account for 
the reworked scheme to be more effective and to cover more number of 
beneficiaries. Further, simplification of procedural requirements for the 
beneficiaries to make use of the scheme’s benefits shall be taken into account 
as part of the revision. 
17. The Committee observe ‘non-receipt of viable proposals’ as a bane in the 
implementation of even many important schemes of Ministry of Textiles 
including the Schemes of Silk sector. The Committee strongly urge that this 
aspect should also be seen by the Ministry for appropriate attention as part of 
the revamping of the scheme.  
JUTE SECTOR 
18. The Committee note that India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute 
products in the world, producing about 90 lakh bales (16 lakh MT) and the 
industry plays a significant role in the Indian economy and provides 
livelihoods for millions. It is estimated that the jute industry provides direct 
employment to 0.40 million workers in organized mills and in diversified units 
including tertiary sector and allied activities and supports the livelihood of 4.0 
million farm families. The Committee find that at present the Indian Jute 
Industry has been facing challenges such as declining demand due to synthetic 
alternatives, lack of modernization in the fields of infrastructure and 
technology, and high production costs due to outdated mills with obsolete 

 
87 
 
technology and infrastructure. The Committee, therefore, are of the considered 
opinion that the Ministry should put in more focus on modernization, 
diversification, and market expansion, while also promoting sustainable 
practices and skill development for both farmers and mill workers. For this the 
Committee exhort the Ministry to explore the possibility of initiating ‘Jute 
Mission’ on the lines of Cotton Mission so that the above mentioned concerns 
could be taken care of more systematically. 
19. The Committee further urge upon the Ministry to organize special 
awareness programmes, in the areas where Jute is majorly grown and 
processed, for making the Mill owners aware about the Amended Technology 
Upgradation Fund (A-TUFS) Scheme of the Ministry of Textiles. This scheme 
would help upgrade existing machinery and install modern looms resulting in 
overall growth and development of farmers and mill workers. The Committee 
also want the Ministry to conduct proper R&D in collaboration with the 
research institutes for developing new innovations for Jute usage. Public 
Private Partnership should be explored as the mode for advancement in this 
direction. The Committee also feel that by the current push of the 
Government to replace plastic with environment friendly packaging options 
should be seen as an opportunity and the Ministry should seek out options 
how jute can fill in the gaps that may be left by plastic bags and other 
synthetic products. Even legislative interventions like amending the Jute 
Packaging Material (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 and 
its robust implementation on the ground could be explored to handhold the 
industry in this endeavour. When it comes to increasing the exports of jute 

 
88 
 
diversified products, the Committee are of the considered opinion that the 
Ministry should probe new international markets other than US, UAE, etc. 
20. The Committee note that Government e-Marketplace (GeM) for Jute and 
jute products is a significant pre-requisite for overall development and growth 
of the Jute Industry in India. As the Ministry have admitted that GeM provides 
increased transparency and also ensures timely payments to the beneficiaries 
by the indenting State Governments, the Committee impress upon the 
Ministry to take pro-active measures to figure out the challenges which are 
there in the existing GeM for the Jute sector. The Committee also desire that 
if need be, the Ministry may get a feedback from the beneficiaries so that the 
difficulties at the grass root level may be alleviated. Considering that GeM 
platform provides innumerable benefits to the buyers as well as the sellers 
such as streamlined procurement, transparency, and increased efficiency for 
government departments and businesses, the Committee hope that it would be 
revisited at the earliest.  
TEXTILE SECTOR 
21. Regarding the specific steps taken to capitalize on the increased 
international textile demands in the face of closure of a number of National 
Textile Corporation (NTC) mills in the country, the Committee find that 
contribution of NTC Mills in overall domestic textile production was very 
minimal (around 1-2 per cent at its peak). The role of NTC Mills in export 
market is almost negligible.  As such, closure of NTC mills would not have any 
bearing on meeting international textile demand.  The Committee, taking note 

 
89 
 
of this scenario, strongly recommend that the Ministry in this situation should 
take extra measures to provide facilitative environment to the textile industry 
in the country by  various appropriate measures which may include more 
remission of duties and taxes on exports to help exporters partially offset their 
production costs to boost up the exports in textiles and apparel and capture 
more share in the international market. 
PM-MITRA 
22. The Committee note that budget is allocated under Capital and Revenue 
Heads for PM-MITRA Scheme and the allocations under Capital Head have been 
utilized in full. The Ministry sought BE of ₹ 300.00 crore in 2024-25 which was 
slashed down to ₹ 44.00 crore at RE stage. Actual Expenditure under the 
Scheme stood at ₹ 24.51 crore as on 25.02.2025.  The Committee are 
concerned to find that the funds under Revenue Head could not be utilized 
during 2024-25 fiscal as these funds are supposed to be released to the seven 
State Governments, only once they fulfill certain criteria including selection of 
Master Developer. As none of the States have selected the Master Developer for 
the PM MITRA Parks, the Government of India share could not be released to 
them; hence there was a shortfall in utilization. This important Scheme was 
launched for a period of seven years from 2021-22 to 2027-28 FY. Taking note 
of the above facts, the Committee express their concern that even after 
passage of five years, only 7 sites in the 7 States have been approved, even the 
construction has not started at all the sites and every year the funds allocated 
for this purpose go unutilized as in 2023-24 wherein   ₹ 0.13 crore was the AE 

 
90 
 
vis-à-vis ₹ 52.30 crore RE. The Committee reckon that PM MITRA is one of the 
most ambitious and prestigious schemes envisioned by the Prime Minister. It 
prima facie appears to the Committee that the lack of initiative by the States 
in providing requisite infrastructure and planning has been one of the reasons 
for the Parks not becoming a reality. The Committee, therefore, recommend 
that the Ministry should take up this matter with the concerned 7 State 
Governments on priority and pursue them to appoint a Master Developer 
within a definite time-line provided by the Ministry. The Committee 
understand that there are difficulties emerging at grass-root level which the 
State Governments have to deal with while completing these Parks. But, 
considering the significance attributed to the Scheme, the Committee 
recommend that a Special Task Force of the representatives of the Central and 
State Governments shall be formed to analyse the teething issues faced by the 
scheme and to suggest practical solutions. Further the Task Force should also 
monitor the progress of PM MITRA Parks and to handhold the States to 
complete the construction of the Parks in the least possible time. This will also 
ensure that the total outlay fixed for the Scheme could be utilised and PM 
MITRA Parks start functioning and provide much needed fillip to the Textile 
Sector . 
23. The Committee expect that the funds of ₹ 300.00 crore at BE stage in FY 
2025-26 would not go unutilized in the ensuing financial year as these Parks 
form part of the vision of future by our PM with the aim of developing 
integrated large scale and modern industrial infrastructure facility for total 
value-chain of the textile industry and are required to be set up by 2027-28 

 
91 
 
with the total expenditure of ₹ 4445.00 crore. Further, the Committee would 
like to be apprised of the total amount utilized out of ₹ 4445.00 crore since the 
launch of the Scheme till date. 
NATIONAL TECHNICAL TEXTILE MISSION (NTTM) 
24. The Committee note that under NTTM, implementation of TSA Hybrid 
model took a considerable time due to which assignment of budget and its 
utilization by respective institutions got delayed. Further, as per the Ministry, 
all R&D Projects involve procurement of instruments and machinery for which 
Capital Budget is allocated. Research Institutions have pointed out that the 
procurement process as per GFR takes significant time due to which the 
assigned amount could not be utilized in timely manner. Taking note of the 
above facts, similar to the recommendation in case of Wool Sector Schemes, 
the Committee urge upon the Ministry of Textiles to take up the specific 
nature of research projects which have extended gestation periods that come 
in the way of adhering to the general fund utilisation pattern as stipulated by 
the Ministry of Finance. Because of this inherent problem, research projects 
require specifically spelt out funding and utilisation guidelines. This may even 
be considered on case-to-case basis. The Committee wants that this aspect 
shall be examined on merit and with the urgency it commands.  
 
 
PLI SCHEME 

 
92 
 
25. The Committee note that PLI Scheme for Textile Sector was launched in 
2020 with an objective of promoting production of MMF Apparel, MMF Fabrics 
and products of Technical Textiles in the country for enabling the Textile 
Sector to achieve size and scale and increase competitiveness. PLI Scheme for 
Textiles has an outlay of ₹ 10,683 crore for a period of five-years. The 
Committee understand that FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24 were gestation period 
for the Scheme and that is why RE of ₹ 7.50 crore was allocated in 2022-23 out 
of which ₹ 7.08 crore were utilized. During FY 2023-24, RE of ₹ 5.00 crore was 
allocated out of which ₹ 4.13 crore could only be made use of. However, the 
Committee cannot but express concern that only ₹ 2.10 crore could be utilized 
in 2024-25 against RE of ₹ 45.00 crore. Though the Ministry apprised the 
Committee that this was because FY 2024-25 is the first performance year 
under the Scheme, the Committee are not satisfied with this reply of the 
Ministry and wonder that if 2025-26 is the first incentive disbursement year, 
then what was the purpose of allocation of funds at RE stage to the tune of ₹ 
45.00 crore in 2024-25. The Committee, however, appreciate the move by the 
Ministry to make amendment in the Scheme guidelines to allow early incentive 
disbursement and expect that the Ministry shall make concerted efforts to 
ensure optimal utilization of the RE funds in 2024-25. 
26. The Committee, taking into consideration that BE 2025-26 has been 
enormously enhanced to ₹ 1148 crore, expect that the PLI Scheme would come 
out of gestation and the Ministry would gainfully and effectively utilize the 
earmarked budget for incentive disbursement to PLI companies in 2025-26 and 
there would be no surrendering of funds at the end of the FY 2025-26. It is 

 
93 
 
pertinent to keep in mind that realizing the purpose of the PLI Scheme of 
expanding manufacturing units in India, generate employment and contribute 
in making the country ‘Aatma-nirbhar’ or ‘self-reliant’ by reducing the imports 
could be achieved only if time over run is prevented.  
27. The Committee note that Ministry of Textiles had submitted two 
proposals viz. PLI 1.2 for expansion of Harmonized System (HS) lines under 
MMF Apparel and MMF fabrics and PLI 2 for apparel/garments, made-ups and 
textiles accessories for making the Scheme more comprehensive. The 
Committee finding the fact that these proposals are still under consideration, 
want that the Ministry should take measures to expedite the 
finalization/approval of these proposal. The Committee also want that the 
Ministry should take well-focused steps to increase the number of PLI 
companies so to promote competitiveness and foreign investments in our 
domestic textile industries. Further, the Committee have taken note of reports 
that the Government is pondering over a decision whether or not to continue 
with the PLI Scheme further. Though facts on this matter have not been placed 
before the Committee, it is observed that the continuance of PLI Scheme or an 
appropriate alternative for Textile Sector would be crucial for facilitating its 
growth in the country.  
 
 
  

 
94 
 
SAMARTH 
28. The Committee note that Scheme for Capacity Building in Textiles Sector 
(Samarth) was initiated from 2017-18 with an aim to incentivize and 
supplement the efforts of the Industry in creation of jobs in the organized 
textile and related sectors, covering the entire value chain of textiles 
(excluding spinning and weaving) with an outlay of ₹ 1300 crore. The Scheme 
was extended for a period of three years, i.e., from 2021-22 to 2023- 2024 with 
an outlay of ₹ 390.00 crore, with the training target of 3.40 lakh candidates 
and further extended to FY 2025-26 with outlay of ₹ 495 crore to train 3 lakh 
persons. The Committee observe that the Ministry had sought BE of ₹ 166.00 
crore for the year 2024-25 under SAMARTH Scheme which was drastically 
revised upwards to ₹ 331.00 crore at RE stage, but the AE was only 153.70 
crore (92 per cent of BE and about 50 per cent of RE) at the end of February, 
2025. However, the Committee find that one lakh persons were to be given 
additional training after the RE stage in 2024-25 and the training of 70,000 
persons is in the final stage which will be completed in February, 2025. The 
Committee understand that as the payments will be released for all these 
trainings in the month of March, 2025, the RE funds would be utilized in  
2024-25 fiscal. The Committee, still are of the firm opinion that Ministry 
should not wait till the fag end of the financial year for the training targets to 
be completed and instead should pace it evenly in batches from the beginning 
of the Financial Year. The Committee believe that the Ministry would make all 
concerted efforts to utilize the RE funds also within the timeline of the FY 
2024-25. 

 
95 
 
29. The Committee are of the considered view that imparting skill 
development training is a continuous process which cannot be stopped after 
one or two years and therefore, recommend the Ministry to take necessary 
measure to continue with this Scheme even after 2025-26 with requisite 
revamping, if required, based on the response received from implementation 
this far. The Committee also desire that the necessary approvals should be 
taken for this at the very beginning of the Financial Year so that the timely 
disbursement of budgetary funds could be carried out and there is no 
underutilisation or diversion of funds.

(i) Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of Labour & Employment;  
 
(ii) Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of Textiles; and  
(iii) Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of Skill Development & 
Entrepreneurship. 
 3. Giving an overview of the important Observations/Recommendations contained in the 
Draft Reports, the Chairperson solicited the views/ suggestions of the Members.  
4. The Committee, then, took up the Draft Reports one by one for consideration.  The 
Chairperson read out the gist of the recommendations contained in the three Reports.  
While the draft Reports on Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment and Ministry of Textiles were adopted without any modifications, the draft 
Report on Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of Skill Development & 
Entrepreneurship was adopted with some modifications.   
 
5. The Committee then authorized the Chairperson to finalise the Reports and present 
the Reports to Parliament on Friday, the 28th March, 2025. 
6. The Chairperson observed that the Report on the subject ‘Implementation of the 
Labour Codes’ need to be presented on priority after thorough examination and taking 
evidence of remaining stakeholders, etc. and requested Members to proactively and 
dispassionately participate in the discussions to be held in near future.   
7. The Committee, thereafter, decided to undertake an on the spot Study Visit to 
Srinagar, Chandigarh and Dharamshala from 5 to 11 June, 2025 to gather first hand 
information at the field level on the subjects selected.  The Committee also decided to have 
their next sitting in the third week of April, 2025. 
  
The Committee then adjourned.

I.  INTRODUCTORY 
 
1.     In the context of technology’s growing role in economic development, skilled 
manpower is essential to drive progress. The Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship (MSDE) collaborates with Central Government Ministries, State 
Governments, industry, non-profits, and academia to synergize and accelerate 
skilling efforts. 
 
2.   This year marks MSDE’s eleventh successful year since its inception in 2014. 
Initially established as the Department of Skill Development under the Ministry of 
Sports & Youth Affairs on 31st July 2014, it was later notified as the Ministry of 
Skill Development & Entrepreneurship on 9th November 2014. Annually, more 
than one crore youth benefit from the Skill India program—a mission aimed at 
equipping youth with skills for better livelihoods. 
 
3.  Over time, MSDE has taken on additional roles through various organizations 
and skilling schemes, including: 
 
Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) 
Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Kendra (PMKK) 
Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) 
Directorate General of Training (DGT) 
National Institute for Entrepreneurship & Small Business Development 
(NIESBUD) 
Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE) 
National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) 
National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) 
 
4.    India, as one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, recognizes the need to 
expand opportunities within service sectors and integrate training courses with 
apprenticeship programs. In December 2014, a significant reform of the 
Apprenticeship Act paved the way for the introduction of the National 
Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS) in August 2016. NAPS strategically 
incentivizes employers to engage more apprentices in their workforce, resulting in 
remarkable advancements in apprenticeship enrollment and active participation 
in skill development over the past ten years. 
 
5.     While skill development is crucial, its impact remains limited unless 
accompanied by employment generation. By fostering the growth of small and 
medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the government plays a pivotal role in creating 
additional employment opportunities and engaging the entire workforce. 
 
6.     MSDE’s mandate includes integrating entrepreneurship orientation modules 
into the Employability, Entrepreneurship, and Life Skills component of PMKVY 
courses. Additionally, ITI courses already incorporate entrepreneurship modules 
within employability skills. To promote a culture of entrepreneurship among 
youth, the Ministry instituted the National Entrepreneurship Awards (NEA) in 
2016, recognizing and honoring outstanding entrepreneurs and ecosystem

builders. These awards serve as models of excellence for others to emulate and 
improve upon.

15.01.2025 is Rs. 895.21 crore, which is 33.33% of BE and 38.61% of RE.

the balance amount of funds amounting to Rs. 1790.43 crore  during the 
remaining part of 2024-25, the Ministry stated as under:-  
 
“The 'Skill India Programme' has been approved by the Cabinet on 
07.02.2025. Following approval, the Ministry has made further releases under the

under the scheme is Rs. 1719.57 Cr, which represents 64% of the BE and 74% of

15.  It was noted that there was persistent increase in the BE during the last 
three years viz. 17.28% in 2023-24, 28.50% in 2024-25 and 34.95% in 2025-26.

not fully utilised.  When asked about the reasons  for the consistent reduction in 
RE as well as shortfall in Actual Expenditure during the last three fiscals,  the 
Ministry stated as follows:-     

 
8 
 
“The Budget Estimates (BE) are proposed based on the approved outlays of 
the Schemes, as well as the anticipated expenditure. During the pre-budget 
exercise, if it is determined that the expenditure under any scheme or unit has 
not progressed as planned, the Ministry proposes to reduce the allocations at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage. Additionally, the Ministry of Finance conducts its 
own assessment and sets ceilings according to their evaluation. Over the past 
three years, the variations in BE, RE, and Expenditure within this Ministry have 
primarily been due to the non-approval of its major scheme 'Skill India 
Programme'. 
  The 'Skill India Programme' is the Ministry's largest scheme, comprising 60-
65% of its total budget. The EFC recommended it on 27.07.2022, and the draft 
Cabinet Note was moved on 23.08.2022. Anticipating approval, projection for RE 
FY 2022-23 and BE 2023-24 was made and approved by the Ministry of Finance. 
Pending Cabinet approval, looking to the crucial need for continuing with skilling 
activities, the Ministry requested permission from DoE to release funds on 
22.11.2022, which was granted on 29.11.2022. Expenditure began in December 
2022, but due to the limited available time in the FY led to low spending. The 
Ministry could spent only Rs. 1387.85 Cr  in FY 2022-23, against a budget 
estimate of Rs. 2999.00 Cr and a revised estimate of Rs. 1901.71 Cr.

A. PRADHAN MANTRI KAUSHAL VIKAS YOJANA (PMKVY4.0)  
28.  MSDE is implementing its flagship scheme Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas 
Yojana (PMKVY), since 2015, for imparting skill development training through 
Short-Term Training (STT) and up-skilling and re-skilling through Recognition of 
Prior Learning (RPL) to youth across the country. It aims to stimulate and 
advance skill development across the country by delivering high-quality, short-
duration training programs in job roles as per the industry requirements. Since 
its inception, three iterations of PMKVY have been successfully implemented, with 
the current phase, PMKVY 4.0, underway. As on 09.01.2025, more than 1.60 
crore candidates have been trained under the PMKVY.  
 
29.  PMKVY 4.0 (2022-26) has been designed with various new elements 
including On-the-job training (OJT), Integration and mainstreaming of vocational 
education with general education as per ‘National Education Policy’ (NEP) 2020, 
offering training in futuristic and new age courses for Industrial Revolution 4.0, 
expanding the delivery network for skill development through cross utilization of 
resources by setting Skill India Centres (SICs) in Institutes of National Repute, 
Schools, Colleges, Universities, Technical Institutions, etc. Under PMKVY 4.0, 
training is being imparted in Short-Term Training (STT), Recognition of Prior 
Learning (RPL) and Special Projects (SP). 
 
The broad design principles of PMKVY 4.0 are: 
 
i. Customized courses with high employability and duration up-to 210 hours. 
ii. Short-Term Training (STT) are by educational institutions (Colleges, 
Schools and Government Institutions), including ITIs to synergize 
vocational and educational streams and increase network of quality 
training providers by increasing partnership of educational and vocational 
institutions. 
iii. Skill courses are selected as per Industry demand. 
iv. Special Projects for identified areas and groups in agriculture, handicraft 
and other traditional sectors. 
v. Skill India Digital Hub (SIDH) platform has been launched for capturing the 
entire training lifecycle. 
vi. Enhanced industry-connect through greater reliance on On-the-Job 
Training in short-term training.  

 
16 
 
vii. Emphasis on re-skilling, and up-skilling under Recognition of Prior 
Learning (RPL) through innovation in assessment and better monitoring. 
viii. Simplified procedures for reducing compliance burden by enlisting multiple 
Assessment Agencies and Awarding Bodies, re-engineering IT systems 
based on requirement of stakeholders, etc. 
ix. Creation of a national pool of trainers and assessors to ensure their 
availability and efficient implementation of training and faster assessment. 
x. Flexibility in course curriculum by introducing courses in partnership with 
industry, other Ministries/Departments, etc. 
xi. Focus on online/digital/blended skilling for effective learning, convenience, 
and outreach. 
xii. Emphasis on community engagement through training in job roles 
addressing the skill needs of the informal sector or basic self-employed. 
xiii. Focus on New Age Skills like Industry 4.0, Web 3.0, AI/ML, AR/VR, 
Climate Change, Circular Economy, Green Economy, and Energy 
Transition.

40. The Committee desired to know as to how the Ministry monitor functioning 
of Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Kendras (PMKKs) and the details of number of 
inspections undertaken during the last three years, deficiencies noticed and steps 
taken to improve their functioning. In reply, the Ministry stated as follow:-      
              
“A robust monitoring framework has been put in place under the Pradhan 
Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) 4.0 scheme to ensure strict monitoring. To 
monitor the effectiveness of the skill training provided under PMKVY, the Ministry 
has launched Skill India Digital Hub (SIDH), a unified platform that integrates 
skilling, education, employment, and entrepreneurship ecosystems to provide a 
life-long array of services targeting a wide range of stakeholders.  
 
Further, the following steps are undertaken to ensure quality standards 
across all training centres, including PMKKs, while imparting training under 
PMKVY 4.0:- 
  
i. The registration process on SIDH ensures e-KYC compliance, Aadhaar based 
authentication of candidate credentials, and mobile number authentication. 
ii. Mandatory Aadhar Enabled Biometric Attendance System (AEBAS). 
iii. Virtual verification of operational training centres using a mobile app, monitor 
remote Training Centres (TCs) locations virtually at any given point of time. 
iv. Call validations are carried out on regular basis for taking feedback of 
candidates on their experiences and support investigation process in case of 
grievances received against Training Partners/Centres. 
v. Physical visits and inspection of the training centre by officials from MSDE and 
State Engagement Officers / other representatives from NSDC are regularly 
undertaken. 
vi. Virtual monitoring through audio and video calls is also conducted by a 
Kaushal Samiksha Kendra set up in MSDE. 
  
Over the last 3 years,a total of 637 Physical Inspections (PIs) have been 
undertaken. The key deficiencies observed during these inspections include non-
conduct of training during visits, PMKKs being closed on working days, non-
compliance with equipment guidelines, candidates being unavailable during visits, 
batch merging, low attendance (below 50%), mismatches between physical 
attendance and AEBAS records, and in some cases, PMKKs not being found at the 
registered address on SIDH.  
          
PMKKs with severe discrepancies are issued Show Cause Notices and 
undergo a Consequence Management process, with penal actions such as 
suspension, financial penalties, and batch cancellations imposed on non-
compliant centres. In order to avoid further occurrence of such discrepancies, 
workshops are also conducted to orient PMKKs on quality delivery of training, 
retention of candidates post mobilization, maintenance of attendance etc.”

B.  JAN SHIKSHAN SANSTHAN (JSS)  
53. The scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan  (JSS), initially launched in 1967 as 
Shramik Vidyapeeth (SVP), aims to provide skill development training in a non-

 
31 
 
formal mode at the doorsteps of the beneficiary through registered Societies 
(NGOs) with 100% grant from the Government of India. The objective of the 
scheme is to increase household income by promoting self/wage employment 
through skill development training.  The skill training is low-cost, flexible, and 
highly accessible to Women, Scheduled Caste (SC), Scheduled Tribe (ST), Other 
Backward Classes (OBCs), minorities, and any other disadvantaged groups of 
society. 
 
54. The target beneficiaries of the scheme are non-literate, neo-literate and the 
person having a rudimentary level of education (70%), school dropouts up to class 
12th (20%), and graduates (10%) in the age group of 15-45 years. Age relaxation 
is given to Divyang and other deserving cases, especially women. The priority 
groups are Women, SC, ST, OBCs and minorities in rural areas and urban low-
income areas.  
 
55 The scheme is implemented through JSSs, functioning under the aegis of 
respective parent bodies. The parent body should register the JSS as a separate 
NGO under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. These JSSs receive financial 
assistance in the form of Grants-in-Aid (GIA) from the Government of India for 
imparting skill training to the assigned target.

65.   When asked to provide the details of specific vocational training and skill 
development initiatives that are being implemented under JSS Scheme and the 
manner in which these initiatives address the needs of marginalized 
communities, the Ministry submitted as follows:-  
“The Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) Scheme, initially launched as Shramik 
Vidyapeeth (SVP) in 1967, aims to provide skill training in a non-formal mode at the 
doorsteps of the beneficiary through registered Societies (NGOs) with 100% grant 
from the Government of India. The objective of the scheme is to increase the 
household income by promoting self/wage employment through skill development 
training. The skill training provided through JSSs is, flexible, affordable and highly 
accessible to women, Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), Other 
Backward Classes (OBCs), minorities, and any other disadvantaged groups of 
society. The target beneficiaries of the scheme are non-literates, neo-literates and 
persons having rudimentary level of education, school dropouts up to class 12th in 
the age group of 15-45 years. Age relaxation is given to Divyangjan and other 
deserving cases, especially women.  
  The following vocational training and skill development initiatives are being 
implemented under the JSS Scheme to address the needs of JSS beneficiaries, 
including marginalized communities: 
Livelihood Cell: Each JSS has a livelihood cell that connects JSS beneficiaries to 
employment, develops entrepreneurship skills, facilitates SHG formation, provides 
credit linkages, etc. 
Creation of Model JSS:Training infrastructure of 30 JSS centers has been 
upgraded for 3 identified job roles Assistant Computer Operator, Assistant Dress 

 
43 
 
Maker, and Beauty Care Assistant under SANKALP project of MSDE. Further, the 
upgradation of 70 more JSSs as Model JSSs is under process. 
Onboarding to SIDH Portal: JSS data has been migrated to the Skill India Digital 
Hub (SIDH) portal, ensuring mobile OTP-based candidate enrollment and 
Aadhaar-based e-KYC for transparency in candidate onboarding and training 
within the JSS ecosystem. 
 
NCVET certification: As the JSS Scheme has been onboarded to SIDH portal, 
from FY 2024-25 onwards, the JSS beneficiaries are now being issued NCVET 
certificate, which consists of QR Code, Credits earned, Beneficiary photo, NSQF 
level, etc. This has enhanced the credibility of JSS certification. 
Courses: 13 new-age NSQF-aligned courses (Level 2/3) have been adopted in the 
FY 2024-25, after approval from the National Council for Vocational Education 
and Training (NCVET). 
Convergence:  JSS scheme has been converged with schemes such as PM 
Vishwakarma Scheme, ULLAS scheme of MoE, Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi 
Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM JANMAN) , Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Unnat Gram 
Abhiyan (PM JUGA) etc 
Capacity Building: Ministry has organized zonal workshops at various locations 
and various capacity-building activities with stakeholders such as the National 
Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development (NIESBUD), the 
Institute of Rural Management, Anand (IRMA), etc, for capacity building of the 
JSSs in the areas such as Linkage with Entrepreneurship, Social Media presence 
and advocacy, Strengthening of Livelihood cells, etc. 
 
Simplifying the Board of Management creation in the JSSs: The affairs of each 
Jan ShikshanSansthan (JSS) are to be managed by a Board of Management that 
represents the interest of the target beneficiaries. JSS has its BoM which acts as 
an administrative body to supervise the functioning of the JSS.  
In order to strengthen the Board of the Management of the JSSs, the 
Ministry has undertaken the following initiatives: - 
- Providing Designation based Government nominations for the 
representatives in the BoM. 
- RDSDE as nominee of the Joint Secretary in the Board of Management of 
the JSSs 
Monitoring: To ensure effective on-ground implementation, the JSS scheme is 
monitored through the SIDH portal and field visits by MSDE and RDSDE officials. 
Udhyam Kart: As a step toward providing a platform to showcase and sell 
products made by JSS beneficiaries and to empower budding entrepreneurs under 
JSS Scheme, a dedicated section for JSS products has been successfully created 
on the UdhyamKart portal, developed by NIESBUD.” 
 
66.  On being asked about the details of measures taken to assess the 
effectiveness of the JSSs programmes in improving the employability and income-
generating capacity of its beneficiaries, the Ministry stated as under:-       
“In order to assess the effectiveness of the JSSs programmes in improving the 
employability and income-generating capacity of its beneficiaries an evaluation 

 
44 
 
study was conducted by Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA) in FY 
2020-21.   
Considering 79% women representation, 50.5% of the rural share, 73.4% change 
in the employment for enhanced livelihood, 89.1% change in the average income of 
each beneficiary, 85.7% mobilization of beneficiaries by JSS, the study team 
recommended the scheme of Jan Shikshan  Sansthan for continuation.” 
 
67. The progress of the JSS Scheme is monitored through the JSS portal and 
the same is being migrated to the new Skill India Digital Hub (SIDH) Portal. When 
asked about the present status and the time by when the exercise is proposed to 
be completed, the Ministry stated as follows:-                                                   
 
  “In order to bring convergence among various skilling efforts across the 
nation, the Skill India Digital Hub (SIDH) is specially designed and developed by 
the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE).  
  From present Financial year onwards, with the approval of the Competent 
Authority, the skill training under the JSS scheme has been successfully 
operational on SIDH portal. This means that entire training life cycle of the 
beneficiary i.e. Enrolment, Batch creation, training, Assessment and Certification 
(NCVET certification) is being carried out on SIDH portal. Migration to SIDH portal 
has ensured Mobile OTP-based candidate enrolment and Aadhar based e-KYC 
ensuring transparency in candidate onboarding and training in the JSS 
Ecosystem. Major monitoring modules under the JSS scheme such as Annual 
Action Plan, Board of Management etc has also been made functional on SIDH. 
The detailed JSS wise data analytics has also been made in form of the Live 
Dashboard on SIDH portal. 
Presently, the existing JSS portal (www.jss.gov.in) is in the last stage of 
migration into the SIDH portal. It is expected that the migration process will be 
completed by March 2025. This migration will strengthen the JSS ecosystem and 
the JSS beneficiaries will also be able to utilize various other benefits of the 
portal.”  
  
C.  NATIONAL APPRENTICESHIP PROMOTION SCHEME (NAPS) - New Version 
 
68. National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS) aims to promote 
apprenticeship training in the country, by providing partial stipend support to the 
apprentices engaged under the Apprentices Act, 1961 and rules thereby. National 
Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS) launched in August 2016 and 
continues as NAPS-2 since 2022-23. Starting August 2023, Direct Benefit 
Transfer (DBT) was launched under NAPS-2. Partial stipend support by GoI 
under NAPS-2 limited to 25% of stipend paid, up to a maximum of Rs.1,500 per 
month, per apprentice is provided during the training period. The stipend support 
by GoI is paid through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to the bank account of 
apprentices.

D.  NATIONAL SCHEME FOR ITIs UPGRADATION  
93. Announced in budget 2024-25, Scheme for upgradation of ITIs aims to 
enhance the quality and outcomes of skilling across India by upgrading 1,000 ITIs 
in a hub-and-spoke arrangement over five years. It will be a new Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme, with a total outlay of Rs.60,000 crore, with contributions 
from the Government of India (Rs.30,000 crore), State Governments (Rs. 20,000 
crore), and the industry, including CSR funding (Rs.10,000 crore). 
 
94. It will involve upgradation of 200 hubs and 800 spoke ITIs, all working 
closely with industry partners to redesign existing courses, introduce new 
courses, along with specialized short-term courses. Additionally, the programme 
includes capacity augmentation of five national institutes for training trainers. 
With these initiatives, it is expected to benefit 20 lakh students over the course of 
five years. A demand of  Rs.5010 crore was placed for FY.2025-26. However 
considering that the scheme is yet at the initial stage, the Ministry of Finance 
agreed for an allocation of Rs.3000.00 crore, for FY.2025-26. 
 
95. It was noticed that for the FY 2025-26, the Gross Demand for Grants for the 
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship is Rs. 8300.10 Cr and the 
net demand is Rs.6100.10 Cr. The demand of Rs. 6100.10 Cr also includes Rs. 
3000.00 Cr for the ‘New ITI Upgradation Scheme’, which is yet to be approved by 
the Cabinet.  The Committee desired to know about the present status of the 
implementation of the Scheme and how the funds earmarked are proposed to be 
utilized during the current fiscal. In response, the Ministry apprised as under:-    
 
“The ‘National Scheme for ITIs Upgradation’ has been recommended by the 
EFC in its meeting held on 9/13.01.2025. The draft Cabinet Note has received the 
approval of Finance Minister on 19.02.2025.  The MSDE is in process of obtaining 
approval of Cabinet Note. Since the approval of the scheme is yet to be obtained, 
the funds could not be released in the FY.2024-25. It is expected that the scheme 
would receive approval in the current FY. Exact amount of release under the 
scheme will depend upon the time available in this FY after the Cabinet approval. 
The allocations in this scheme have been reduced to Rs. 294.00 Cr  at the RE 
stage. Meanwhile, pending the Cabinet approval, the Ministry has been permitted 
to spend only Rs. 10 Cr on the preparatory activities of the scheme.”

“The New ITI Upgradation Scheme was announced in Union Budget 2024-
25. The initial BE of Rs. 1,000 crore was announced as part of the Budget

“The new scheme is being designed on the principles of Investment (need-
based and industry-relevant); Decentralization (aligned with industrial clusters 
and the local economy); Governance (industry-managed, outcome-based 
institutions, with accountability dovetailed with autonomy); and Trainer 
Development (scaling up NSTIs for trainer/professional development). MSDE has 
undertaken wide stakeholder consultation involving industries, State/UT 
governments, and inter-ministerial consultation, along with Workshops for 
Technical Knowledge Exchange with four countries (China, Germany, Singapore, 
and South Korea) to arrive at the design of the scheme. The scheme is proposed to 
be launched in March 2025.” 
 
98.    On being asked  about the status of the approval of the Scheme by the 
Cabinet and the preparedness/plan of action to utilize the funds earmarked for 
2024-25, the Ministry stated as follows:-     
“The approval of the Scheme by the Cabinet is currently in process. The 
Expenditure Finance Committee, in its meetings held on 09.01.2025 and 
13.01.2025, recommended the approval of the Scheme. The Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship is in the process of finalizing the Cabinet Note 
for approval. Since the Scheme has not yet been approved, the allocated funds 
could not be utilized in FY 2024-25. However, a Revised Estimate of Rs.294 crore 

 
62 
 
has been proposed to be utilized for initiating the implementation of the Scheme 
once approval is obtained.” 
99. The representative of the Ministry during evidence deposed as under:   
“The next xxx is with regard to the budgetary status of National Scheme of 
ITI's Upgradation. Budget estimates for 2024-25 was Rs.1,000 crores. In the 
revised estimates, we were given Rs.294 crore, but ultimately, pending Cabinet 
approval, DOI has permitted to spend only Rs.10 crores in the National Scheme of 
ITI upgradation for preparatory activities. The status of the scheme is that as of 
now the draft Cabinet note has been approved by the Finance Minister, and the 
Ministry is in the process of obtaining Cabinet approval.”  
100. The representative of the Ministry during evidence supplemented as under:   
“Secondly, the new scheme of ITI is quite an ambitious scheme. We are in 
the final stage of it. We have taken the approval of the Department of Expenditure 
as well as the approval of the Finance Minister. The new scheme which has been 
announced in this budget, which is about the five centres of excellence, efforts are 
being made to link them with this scheme. When we link both, our scheme will be 
approved. We have progressed a lot in that. Our guidelines are also being 
prepared. We have also talked to the state government and the industry so that we 
can give momentum to this scheme. We have structured this scheme keeping in 
mind our ITI system. We will try our best to improve the ITI infrastructure wise 
under the control of the state with the cooperation of the industry. We can de-
regulate them, give them freedom and strengthen their governance structure, we 
have edited this scheme keeping all these things in mind.”  
 
101.   The Scheme involves upgradation of 1000 ITIs in hub-and spoke 
arrangement i.e. 200 hubs and 800 spoke ITIs.  When asked about the criteria for 
selecting ITIs for upgradation, especially in terms of infrastructure, course 
contents, alignment with industry needs etc. the following information was 
furnished by the Ministry:-   
 
“The ITIs will be identified by State Governments in consultation with the 
industries and as per the guidelines issued by MSDE. It is informed that MSDE is 
in the process of preparing the scheme guidelines.” 
 
102.  The Committee were apprised that the key role of States/UTs will be 
identification of clusters.  It was also informed that the governance of the Scheme 
will be  Industry managed.  When asked to clarify as to how the Ministry will 
coordinate and monitor these aspects, the Ministry in their subsequent written 
reply stated as follows:-  (Post Evi.First Batch LoP 19)  
“The ITI falls under the administrative control of the State/UT government. 
Therefore, States/UTs serve as the primary drivers of the scheme, including the 
responsibility for cluster identification. Similarly, as announced in the Union 
Budget 2024 regarding the upgradation of 1,000 ITIs under a hub-and-spoke 
model with an outcome-oriented approach, the course content and design will be 

 
63 
 
aligned with industry skill needs. Consequently, an industry-led governance 
structure has been proposed.  
Regarding the role of the Central Government, the scheme will be 
monitored by the National Steering Committee, headed by the Secretary, MSDE. 
This committee will play a key role in finalizing operational guidelines, monitoring 
progress, and recommending necessary course corrections. Furthermore, the final 
approval of the Strategic Investment Plan, as recommended by the States, will be 
granted by the Centre. The Central Government will also monitor Key Performance 
Indicators (KPIs) through third-party evaluations and conduct regular meetings to 
track implementation progress.”                                             
103. When asked as to what extent the new Scheme is expected to supplement 
the infrastructure deficiencies in the skilling of manpower in the country and 
cater to the needs of emerging sectors like electronics, renewable energy and 
automation to meet the skills demand in both the national and global job 
markets, the Ministry responded as under:-  
 
“The scheme proposes a hub and spoke model for upgradation of ITIs. A 
hub ITI will have, on an average, four (4) spoke ITIs. Upgraded ITIs are envisioned 
to be equipped with state-of-the-art infrastructure, machinery, and equipment, 
with proper space and facility planning for procurement and placement of required 
lab resources as per the course and curriculum plan. It will ensure that the 
students receive high-quality learning through modern facilities and up-to-date 
equipment, all of which making the ITIs aspirational. On an average, four (4) new 
courses would be introduced, and ten (10) existing courses would be upgraded at 
the hub ITIs. On an average, two (2) new courses would be introduced, and eight 
(8) existing courses would be upgraded in spoke ITIs. The newly introduced trades 
will cater to the emerging sectors like electronics, renewable energy and 
automation to meet the skills demand in both the national and global job 
markets.” 
 
104.  On being asked to provide details of the proposed mechanism to monitor 
and assess the likely impact of the proposed New ITIs Upgradation Scheme on the 
skilling and employment outcomes of the youth in the country, the Ministry 
submitted as under:-  
“Yes, there will be a detailed monitoring framework for the scheme, which 
will be tracked. The scheme will focus on results in two complementary ways. 
First, it will provide a monitoring framework that will include ambitious targets 
and cover inputs, outputs, outcomes, timelines, measurement parameters, 
mechanisms for measurement, and validation. It will focus strengthening 
governance, industry linkages, infrastructure, and training to ensure alignment 
with evolving industry needs.    
To ensure accountability, each hub-and-spoke cluster will be required to 
submit a comprehensive Strategic Investment Plan (SIP) upfront, adhering to the 
provided template. These plans will include measurable parameters for inputs, 
outputs, and outcomes, along with timelines. Progress will be closely monitored, 
through regular reporting and reviewed against these predefined metrics.  
Second, the funding under the scheme will be provided on a performance 
basis, i.e., when certain key performance indicators are achieved. These key 

 
64 
 
performance indicators will be Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLIs) specified in 
results-based loans from the World Bank and ADB and will cascade down from 
the Centre to States to ITIs. 
Moreover, the World Bank and ADB will bring expertise in supporting the 
Ministry to carry out an impact evaluation of the scheme. The combination of this 
impact evaluation and the independent verification of the achievement of DLIs will 
provide robust evidence of the success of the scheme. 
To support implementation and tracking, a five-year investment plan and a 
set of performance indicators for measuring success will be included as part of 
scheme guidelines.”

Entrepreneurship Programme is as under: 
 
The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) in 
collaboration with NITI Aayog and Women Entrepreneurship Platform (WEP) as 
knowledge partner, has launched the Swavalambini Women Entrepreneurship 
Programme on 07th February 2025 in North Eastern states of India as Meghalaya, 
Mizoram and Assam.  
The Swavalambini Project is designed to foster an entrepreneurial mindset 
among women students, making them aware of the available support 
mechanisms, schemes, resources, and networks necessary to pursue 
entrepreneurship as a career. The project will also be launched as a pilot in 
selected colleges and universities of Uttar Pradesh and Telangana. The National 
Institute of Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development (NIESBUD) and 
Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE) shall be the implementing partners for 
the pilot project. 
1. Implementation Period 
The Swavalambini Women Entrepreneurship Programme will be 
implemented in selected colleges and HEIs, ensuring adequate time for planning, 
execution, and monitoring across all phases. The programme will include Faculty 
Development Programmes (FDP) of 5 days for selected faculty members from 
colleges, Entrepreneurship Awareness Programmes (EAP) of 2 days for 1,200 
students, Entrepreneurship Development Programmes (EDP) of 40 hours for 
selected 600 students, followed by 6 months of mentoring and handholding 
support to ensure sustained guidance and business development assistance. 
2. Criteria for Selection of Universities and Students 
 Universities & Colleges Selection Criteria: 

 
73 
 
The selection of institutions for this initiative will prioritize those with a 
well-established ecosystem for entrepreneurship and innovation, ensuring a 
strong foundation for fostering startups and business ventures. Additionally, the 
availability of dedicated faculty and institutional support for entrepreneurship 
programs will be considered in the selection process. Furthermore, institutions 
with the potential for scaling the initiative within their academic framework will be 
preferred, allowing for long-term sustainability and broader impact. 
 Student Selection Criteria: 
A customized online application form will be created and hosted on Skill 
India Digital Hub (SIDH) portal and the WEP platform for initial selection of the 
1200 students from the selected colleges.All the selected candidates shall also be 
registered on the NIESBUD portal/IIE portal and on SIDH which will track the 
complete life cycle of the trainee and provide inputs on its progress.  
Selected Institutions participating in the will also disseminate the 
application form through their internal communication channels.Faculties trained 
through Faculty Development Programme shall support in mobilizing the students 
for the programme. 
The selection mechanism for the Entrepreneurship Awareness Programme 
(EAP) and the Women Entrepreneurship Development Programme (WEDP) will 
follow a structured and merit-based approach.  
 Initially, collaboration with participating institutions will be undertaken to 
identify and finalize the top 1,200 applicants (150 from each institution) for 
the EAP.  
 To assess entrepreneurial interest and potential, a well-designed Aptitude 
Test will be developed and administered to all EAP participants.  
 Based on the test results, the top 600 candidates will be selected for the 
WEDP. 
 Additionally, a Selection Committee will be constituted to oversee the 
shortlisting process, ensuring transparency and fairness. Regular meetings 
will be organized to review applications and finalize the list of selected 
candidates. 
3. Preparedness of Implementing Agencies (IAs) 
 The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) has been 
working for promoting entrepreneurship development amongst women, 
marginalized communities, and individuals from lower socio-economic 
backgrounds in the country through its autonomous Institutes, namely, 
National Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development 
(NIESBUD), Noida and Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati.  
 Both the institutes deliver Entrepreneurship Awareness Programmes (EAP), 
Entrepreneurship Development Programmess (EDP), Faculty Development 
Programmes (FDP), Entrepreneurship and Skill Development Programmes 
(ESDP) along with Mentoring and handholding support to aspiring and 
existing entrepreneurs across the country through their centres and in 
partnership with various other stakeholders. 
 Over the past ten years, both NIESBUD and IIE have collectively trained 
12,33,699 candidates through various programs and interventions, 

 
74 
 
demonstrating their significant contribution to the entrepreneurial 
ecosystem. Notably, 7,06,617 (57.27%) of these trainees have been women, 
highlighting their commitment to promoting women’s entrepreneurship and 
inclusive economic growth. 
4. Budgetary Allocation 
 The estimated budget for the program includes funding for faculty training, 
student training, mentorship support, outreach, and operational costs. 
 Financial provisions for seed funding and awards for high-potential 
startups will be facilitated with the support of NITI Aayog under the Award 
to Reward (ATR) Initiative. 
 Budgetary details will be finalized based on institutional agreements and 
approvals. 
5. Tentative Intake in Each University/College 
The target intake is 1,200 female students under the Entrepreneurship 
Awareness Programme (EAP), with a further selection of 600 students for the 
Women Entrepreneurship Development Programme (WEDP).  
The specific intake for each university/college will be determined based on 
institutional capacity and interest levels. 
6. Plan of Action for Implementation of the Four Phases 
 Phase I: Faculty Development Program (FDP) (5 Days) 
o Train selected faculty members from participating institutions. 
o Ensure trained faculty are equipped to guide students effectively. 
 Phase II: Entrepreneurship Awareness Programme (EAP) (2 Days) 
o Mobilize students with the support of trained faculty. 
o Conduct awareness sessions for 1,200 students. 
 Phase III: Women Entrepreneurship Development Programme (WEDP) 
(40 Hours) 
o Selection and Identification of 600 students for advanced entrepreneurship 
training. 
o Training to focus on six key areas as entrepreneurial skills, access to 
finance, market linkages, compliance and legal requirements, mentoring 
and networking, and business development services to prepare these 
students for a career as an entrepreneur. 
 Phase IV: Mentoring and Handholding Support (21 Weeks: 2-3 Hours 
Per Week) 
o Provide personalized mentorship and industry exposure for the trained 
students. 
o Facilitate access to funding, incubation, and market opportunities with the 
support of NITI Aayog and WEP. 

 
75 
 
o Recognize and showcase successful women entrepreneurs.”

“The National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF) alignment and 
approval of qualifications is a dynamic process wherein the qualifications are 
approved periodically in accordance with the industry requirements for imparting 
need-based skill trainings. The NSQF aligned and approved qualifications are 

 
81 
 
reflected in the National Qualification Register (NQR) portal, which is a centralized 
repository for all such qualifications.  
To maintain the relevance and currency of these qualifications, the 
qualifications are approved with a validity period of 3 years, unless otherwise 
specified by the NSQC. Upon completion of this period, the qualifications are 
revised by incorporating necessary technological and other changes.  
Additionally, to ensure that only relevant and industry driven qualifications 
remain active in the skilling ecosystem, NCVET follows the prescribed process of 
periodical archival of qualifications which fall under the below mentioned criteria: 
a) The validity of the qualification has expired and the awarding bodies 
concerned have not taken up the same for revision, hence all such qualifications 
are deemed to be not required in the skill ecosystem. 
b) Any entity which had got the qualifications NSQF aligned either during the 
time of NSDA or till 2021 with NCVET and is presently not a recognized awarding 
body (AB) of NCVET. 
c) All such Qualifications where there is no training conducted and/or are 
inactive for more than a year. 
d) Qualifications which have not been rationalized as per the National Credit 
Framework (NCrF) and revised National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF).  
e) The NCVET recognized awarding body has requested deactivation/archiving 
of their qualifications.  
Accordingly, the NSQC in its meetings, based on the criteria above, 
undertakes regular archival of qualifications. Based on this, as on date (till 41st 
NSQC), a total of 8151 qualifications have been NSQF aligned and approved of 
which 5062 qualifications have been archived so far. Presently, 3089 NSQF 
aligned and approved qualifications are valid and active.”

V. DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF TRAINING 
122.   It has been noticed that there were 15,012 ITIs in 2023-24 viz-a-viz 14,619 
in 2024-25 i.e. there is reduction of 393 ITIs. Similarly, there is reduction in the 
number of seats from 26 lakhs in 2023-24 to 23.17 lakhs in 2024-25. When the 
Committee asked the reasons for reduction in the number of ITIs as well as the 
number of seats, the Ministry in their subsequent written reply stated as under:-               
                                                     
“The Directorate General of Training has introduced an objective 
methodology for grading of Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) from 2023.  This 
Data Driven Grading Methodology (DDGM) is based on several parameters 
available in the DGT-MIS portal, on the basis of which ITIs are awarded 
numerical grading.  
While implementing this methodology, discrepancies have been found in 
the data, especially regarding the number of seats in ITIs which were found to be 
lying vacant for several years. This was affecting the grading of an ITI, as 
‘admission percentage’ which is an important criterion in the DDGM gets 
wrongly reflected. Further, sanitization and accuracy of data is also essential for 
preparation of the correct seat matrix for admission and furnishing of 
information to various important forums. 
As per DGT letter no. DGT-12/01/2018-TC (Part) dated 20.12.2018, any 
trade or unit with zero admissions for two consecutive years will be deactivated. 
DGT granted a one-time relaxation in 2022 for ITIs with 100% vacant seats for 
two consecutive years due to the Covid-19 pandemic. 
To optimize seating capacity, DGT conducted a review to identify seats 
continuously vacant for five years. After considering representations from ITIs 
and State Directorates, a total of 4,49,636 seats in 5358 ITIs were de-affiliated 
starting from 17.01.2025. This reduced seating capacity to 23.17 lakh and the 
number of ITIs to 14619 in 2024-25.”

124. The Committee noticed that in the context of Integration of Skilling with 
Education Level, it has been proposed to embed skilling at secondary, senior 
secondary, and higher education levels to ensure that it is aspirational, it has 
seamless mobility between formal education and vocational training.  When 
asked whether the Ministry have any proposal for skilling of school dropouts at 
various levels, the Ministry in their subsequent written stated as under:-                                 
“Under PMKVY 4.0, school dropouts at various levels are already covered 
with multiple job roles provisioning for school drop-outs as eligible candidates for 
training. Further PMKVY 4.0 aligns with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 
by embedding vocational education in secondary, senior secondary, and higher 
education levels.  
Key initiatives taken to promote skilling in educational institutions are as 
follows: 
 Flexibility and mobility in education through National Credit 
Framework(NCrF) -The National Credit Framework (NCrF) allows students to 
accumulate and store learning credits in the Academic Bank of Credit (ABC), with 
APAAR IDs generated to uniquely identify and track each learner’s academic 
progress, ensuring flexibility and multiple entry-exit options. This enables 
seamless mobility across institutions, helping students transfer and redeem 
credits for continued education. By recognizing diverse learning forms, NCrF 
enhances career opportunities and supports lifelong learning. 
 Cross-utilization of infrastructure to impart skilling in educational 
institutes- The existing infrastructure available with education ecosystem 
including schools and Higher Education Institute has been effectively utilized for 
running Skill India Centres (SICs) in different educational institutions including 
Schools (such as Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya, Kendri Vidyalaya, CBSE schools, 
Cantonment schools, PM Shri Schools, etc.), UGC approved 
Colleges/Universities, Skill Universities, AICTE affiliated Engineering and 
technical institutes, etc.”

I. FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE 
 
1.   The Committee note that the BE for 2024-25 was  Rs.4520.00 crore 
whereas the revised estimate for the year was reduced to  Rs. 3300.83 
crore, out of which the Ministry were able to spend only Rs. 2226.13 crore 
(as on 18.02.2025) which is 49.25% of BE and 67.44% of RE. For the 
shortfall in utilisation of funds, the Ministry attributed factors like delay in 
approval of Skill India Programme (SIP) and the National Scheme for ITIs 
Upgradation. The Ministry also stated that during the remaining period of 
2024-25, around Rs. 598 crore is expected to be released in SIP alone and 
around Rs. 180 crore in SANKALP scheme apart from other expenditure. 
The Committee have been apprised that at present, approval of the Cabinet 
is awaited for the National Scheme for ITI Upgradation.  
 
   The Committee observed that there was persistent increase in the BE 
during the last three years viz. 17.28% in 2023-24, 28.50% in 2024-25 and 
34.95% in 2025-26. However, since 2022-23, every year BE was reduced at 
RE stage, which was also not fully utilised. In response, the Ministry have 
stated that over the past three years, the variations in BE, RE, and 
Expenditure within the Ministry have primarily been due to the non-
approval of its major Scheme viz. 'Skill India Programme', which comprises 
60-65% of its total budget for which the Department of Economic Affairs 
was requested from time to time for fund releases.  
The Committee further note that the BE for SIP during 2024-25 is 
Rs.2685.64 crore which was reduced to Rs.2318.00 crore at RE stage. The 
actual expenditure as on 03.03.2025 is Rs.1719.57 crore (PMKVY 4.0-
Rs.1271.10 crore against RE of Rs.1538 crore; JSS-Rs.72.62 crore against 
RE of Rs.180 crore and PM-NAPS Rs.375.85 crore against RE of Rs.600 
crore) which is 64% of the BE and 74% of RE of the scheme. The Ministry
